title: There’s always been more than one route to becoming a professor
summary: Winston Morgan explains there's more than one route to a professorship – the real question is why there are still so few Black professors
full_text:
For reasons that readers will be familiar with, this summer’s media coverage of higher education has seen one conversation after another about what it means to be appointed as a professor.

It is important to point out that not all professorial appointments are the same – and nor do they need to be.

While many people talk about professorial appointments, relatively few truly understand the process and why such appointments are made. In part, this is because academic promotion and appointment procedures are often opaque, even to those working within higher education.

When is a professor a professor?

Before discussing how professors are appointed, it is worth clarifying what is meant by a Professor or Full Professor, as distinct from an Assistant Professor or Associate Professor.

A Full Professor holds the highest academic rank within a university and broadly speaking, there are three equally valid routes to attaining this position.

The traditional and most widely recognised route is through academic achievement. Appointments are based primarily on an individual’s research output, including both the quality and quantity of publications, demonstrating a significant contribution to their field. Other important criteria include excellence in teaching, leadership in research, supervision of doctoral students, postdoctoral researchers, and other academics, as well as the ability to generate research income for the institution. Individuals who meet these criteria typically establish strong national and often international reputations and are recognised as experts in their discipline.

Appointments through this route are usually assessed by an internal university panel, supported by external members and informed by references from several established professors who can objectively evaluate the candidate against clearly published criteria. This process is most commonly used for internal promotions and therefore must adhere to rigorous human resources and equality standards.

While this is how the process is intended to work, many academics can point to examples where individuals have been appointed despite not fully meeting every aspect of the expected criteria.

A second route to a professorship is through appointment to a senior academic leadership position, such as Head of Department, Dean, or Pro Vice-Chancellor. In these cases, the professorial title may be attached to the role itself, reflecting the responsibilities and strategic significance of the position.

A third route exists where a university’s leadership decides, for strategic reasons, to appoint an individual to a professorship. This may be done to strengthen an emerging field of research, support institutional transformation, address workforce needs, or tackle long-standing structural inequalities. In these circumstances, universities may exercise greater flexibility and appoint individuals who do not yet satisfy the full range of traditional professorial criteria.

The purpose of such appointments is not to lower standards but to recognise a different set of strengths which are believed to have equal validity. These appointments are typically based on an individual’s unique expertise, leadership potential, professional impact, or ability to help the institution achieve specific strategic objectives. They are often targeted at external candidates or younger academics whose career trajectories indicate exceptional promise, even if they have not yet accumulated the conventional portfolio associated with a traditional professorship.

Given the nature of these appointments, it is not appropriate to judge such individuals solely against the criteria used for traditional promotion-based professorships. They are appointed for different reasons, fulfil different roles, and are expected to deliver against different, though equivalent, measures of success.

As we have seen, these appointments can sometimes create frustration among traditionally appointed academics, particularly when institutions fail to communicate clearly the rationale behind them. Without transparency regarding the justification, selection process, and expected outcomes, appointees can find themselves isolated and forced to defend their legitimacy, especially when their appointment becomes associated with broader political or social debates.

Ultimately, the decision to appoint someone as a professor rests with the university itself, not the appointee, although institutions generally seek to maintain standards that are comparable across the sector.

Addressing underrepresentation

One area where strategic appointments may be particularly relevant is the continuing underrepresentation of Black professors in UK higher education. While students from global majority backgrounds comprise a significant proportion (28 per cent) of the student population, representation at the most senior academic levels remains disproportionately low with only one per cent or about 250 Black professors when there should be four per cent or 1000 Black professors given the population breakdown.

To deliver on their core objectives, universities increasingly recognise the need for a broader range of academics, researchers, perspectives, and research agendas. Achieving this goal is unlikely if appointments continue to be drawn from a narrow and historically homogeneous pool of candidates. Borrowing a concept from genetics, diversity increases the capacity of a system to adapt, innovate, and succeed.

What remains clear, however, is that many UK universities have struggled to articulate the business and academic case for diversity. Too often, institutions rely solely on social justice arguments, which some audiences perceive as political rather than strategic. If universities are to make professorial appointments intended to address structural imbalances, including the underrepresentation of Black professors, they must clearly explain why such appointments are necessary, the objectives they serve, and the value they are expected to deliver both within the institution and beyond it.

Only through greater transparency can universities maintain confidence in the professorial title while ensuring that academic excellence, leadership, innovation, and institutional transformation are all recognised as legitimate pathways to professorship.

Asking Black professors about their journey is expected and beneficial. But given the different appointment processes and the fact that we can dismiss the genetics arguments as pseudoscience, the scale of the underrepresentation needs to be explained and addressed.

In this context, the more important question we should all be asking the university sector and wider society is not how someone became a professor but where are the 750 missing Black professors?

full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Maureen Graham, Senior Lecturer in Initial Teacher Education, University of Hertfordshire.

‘A new broom sweeps clean’ they say, and Andy Burnham’s new UK government has wasted little time in announcing radical educational reforms. After only two weeks in office, plans are being made to move away from the current “one size fits all” system of secondary education and introduce alternative technical education pathways for pupils from the age of 14.

The rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) provides a compelling reason to think differently, and many teachers and parents will already recognise that not every young person thrives in an academic environment. Giving pupils the opportunities to develop vocational and technical skills alongside the core subjects of English, mathematics and science could provide meaningful, alternative routes into employment.

No details have as yet emerged on the exact role that schools will play; however, given that all pupils attend mandatory school education until 16, the school curriculum in terms of offering and uptake will inevitably be affected. Changing what young people learn inevitably raises questions:

Who will teach the new subjects?

What happens to those subjects struggling in an already crowded curriculum?

What might these reforms mean for higher education institutes educating many of England’s future teachers?

Shrinking pools

Recent government data show a longer term upward trend for exam entries at both GCSE and A Levels. However, even with a rise in pupil numbers, these headline figures conceal considerable differences between subjects. Geography, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, French and Computing have experienced declining exam entries for reasons beyond pupil preferences, such as curriculum structures and specialist staff availability.

Pupils opting for new technical pathways may result in even smaller cohorts in some subjects, including those core sciences. Over time, this could reduce demand for specialist teachers. Whilst this could alleviate England’s struggles to recruit sufficient teachers, smaller cohorts mean reduced university enrolments and reduced income. At what point does a small subject cohort become financially unviable? There is already a wider backdrop of financial instability across UK higher education, and if teacher education cohorts continue to contract, how many universities will continue to regard small, specialist teacher-training programmes as sustainable? Teacher education programmes cannot be switched on and off in response to short-term fluctuations in pupil numbers. If university provision in a subject closes, expertise, experienced teacher educators and school partnerships may also disappear. Should demand increase, rebuilding that infrastructure may prove harder than dismantling it. However, technical education needs teachers too.

Who will teach these new pathways?

Engineers and builders could bring valuable professional knowledge into schools but trade expertise does not necessarily equate to teaching expertise. Understanding how to sequence learning, explain complex ideas, assess understanding, respond to the very different needs of 14-year-olds (a current government focus) whilst maintaining safeguarding protocols requires pedagogical and professional expertise as well as technical skills.In England, established routes into teaching normally involve Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), requiring trainees to demonstrate that they meet Teacher Standards. Teacher training is also underpinned by the government’s Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework (ITTECF), which sets out a common entitlement to knowledge and practice in areas including subject and curriculum knowledge, classroom practice, assessment, adaptive practice and behaviour.

So where will technical teachers sit within this professional framework? Will industry experts be expected to train towards QTS and the same professional standards as other teachers, or will alternative routes be developed? If industry specialists are to become technical educators, who will support them in transforming occupational expertise into knowledge that can be taught effectively to young people?

There is a potential paradox with these reforms. A more diverse curriculum could require a broader range of specialist teachers and greater, not less, expertise in teacher preparation. Yet this is happening at a time when university-based teacher education is already experiencing considerable change and, in some cases, contracting provision.

There may also be a longer-term ripple effect. If fewer pupils pursue particular academic subjects at 14 and 16, fewer may progress to university to study them. University departments could face declining numbers in the disciplines from which future specialists are drawn. This raises a problematic question: in expanding technical choice, how do we ensure England retains sufficient academic pathways and disciplinary expertise for those young people who wish to pursue them? How might these changes then affect the breadth of academic study available to English pupils compared with their peers internationally?

A new broom may indeed sweep clean, and providing young people with meaningful alternatives to traditional academic pathways could be an important and overdue reform. But before we sweep too vigorously, we might want to consider what we keep.

The bigger question is whether policies are being considered collectively. Curriculum reform changes what pupils study and to what level; which affects the teachers needed; which affects recruitment into teacher education; which affects universities’ financial stability. Universities need undergraduates; their entry depends on subject A levels; which are dependent on school provision, which responds to demand.

Policies may seem perfectly reasonable when considered individually; but combined, their consequences look rather different.

full_text:
One of the highlights of the summer before college was trotting off to my local Linens N Things to outfit my new home, a triple dorm room in the Little Building at Emerson College in Boston. Armed with a list of must-haves and strongly suggested essentials, I filled a shopping cart with a lot of stuff I’d use immediately (jersey twin XL sheets) and stuff that I’d eventually throw away after four years (the very same sheets, useless after college when you will never see a twin XL bed again.)

Most, if not all, of the stuff I bought didn’t make it out of Boston, save for a pop-up laundry hamper that did a tour of duty in San Francisco, surviving three moves in four years, before being relegated to its final resting place, the garbage can.

But not all college buys need to be destined for the dumpster. For some graduates, items they bought to get through college have not only carried them well into adulthood, they have inadvertently turned into some of their most-cherished things. We asked college grads from 27 to 57 about the things they bought, loved and still use today, from the ubiquitous under-bed storage to a box that perfectly fits a deck of tarot cards.

And, in some cases when the exact items they’ve shared weren’t always available, we recommended alternatives that we think measure up to the original.

Shannon Melero, 34, graduated from SUNY Oswego in 2013

My item is … a fleece blanket.

I don’t know that I picked this out myself because I’m not a paisley girl, but when shopping for school, I remember my mom and I were really fixated on items that would be warm and cozy because I was traveling so far up north for the first time.

I wouldn’t say it’s special, but it’s one of those items that has just endured a lot of high and low moments. I was under that blanket when I got pulled out of my dorm room by EMTs because of bad pneumonia. That blanket was on the couch of the first apartment I shared with my husband. It was cozy and nice but not so nice that I felt like I couldn’t use it. I lay it out on the floor to make a little bed for my daughter to watch TV sometimes. Or if it’s cold, I’ll wrap it around my legs. If it starts to smell too much like my dogs and becomes un-cleanable, I will replace it.

Stella Gewirz, 27, graduated from Denison University in 2021

My item is … an under-bed storage drawer.

… and a stepladder

These two items I bought in college thinking they were gonna be kind of stupid but have ended up being incredibly useful through my adult life! I used to use this as under-bed storage and have since purchased a table top for it to use as bathroom storage/table. The step stool is pretty self-explanatory but has especially come in handy for hanging curtains and new light fixtures (which 18-year-old me would have never imagined!)

I’d say neither is particularly mind blowing but I wasn’t aware of the importance that long-lasting practical items would have on my life until I entered the real world. I moved four times in college (all in dorms) and three times since graduating (twice cross country) and both of these items have stayed with me the entire time. I currently use the rack for bathroom storage and have since purchased another for extended hall closet storage. I probably would only replace the step stool if I found one that was equally sturdy, but 10,000x more chic.

Sarah Holm, 29, graduated from Ohio University in 2018

My item is … a bright yellow, pink and blue ENO DoubleNest Hammock.

I picked out my hammock from a local outdoor store for my 19th birthday in August 2015. It was right before my sophomore year started. During my first year on campus, I noticed students using hammocks everywhere, so I wanted to try one for myself.

That hammock ended up being my go-to place to study and relax between classes, a quiet retreat from the rowdy dorms and a free way to spend time with friends. My highlighter yellow hammock became a beacon for my buddies to spot me across campus and come over for a quick chat or spontaneous hang. I loved it so much that I started our school’s first ever Hammock Club as a simple way to encourage students to spend time outside together.

After 11 years, that hammock is still kickin’! It lives in the trunk of my car so I am ready to hammock whenever I have two trees and 20 minutes. My love for this hammock led me to get my first “real” job out of college with the company that makes them, ENO. I moved from my home state of Ohio to North Carolina, and have worked here for over six years. It’s astounding to look at the life I have built for myself and be able to trace it all back to that one birthday present.

Nikita Khanderia, 24, graduated from the College of William and Mary in 2024

My item is … a laundry hamper.

I bought it for the very unglamorous purpose of hauling laundry around in college. Years later, I’m the founder and CEO of ERIA, a hospitality and events company, and that same basket has ended up carrying extension cords, signage, emergency supplies and whatever else we suddenly need while producing an event.

There is something very humbling about producing a beautiful, high-end event and then arriving behind the scenes with a college laundry basket full of supplies. I keep thinking I should replace it, but at this point it has survived college, multiple moves, starting a company and more event emergencies than I can count. It may actually be the most reliable employee I have.

The funny part is that the laundry basket has evolved into a real thing at ERIA. My entire job is essentially risk mitigation. I’m constantly thinking, “What could a client possibly need that we don’t have?”

So the basket became my just in case basket. It has everything from blister supplies and perfume to detergent sticks and all sorts of bizarre little things a bride, guest or client might suddenly need. If something goes wrong, I want us to have already thought of it.

Diana Budds, 39, graduated from UC Davis in 2008

My item is … a 10-piece All-Clad copper-core cookware set (AKA the Cadillac of cookware sets).

It was a gift from my parents my sophomore year. I begged them for it! (I also really wanted a car, but there was absolutely no way I was going to get that, and this seemed like the kind of useful, buy-it-for-life thing I could convince them to get me.) I’ve always loved to cook – one of my favorite shows growing up was Jacques & Julia: Cooking at Home – and wanted equipment that worked well.

I still have every piece, and use them whenever I cook. I actually have a lot of kitchen items that have proven their worth through many move-related purges. The useful things continue to be useful and I value that a lot. There was a time where I thought I would have to replace a skillet after a roommate burned the hell out of what she cooked in it. But thankfully, elbow grease and Bar Keepers Friend made it shine (almost) like new.

Leopoldo Villardi, 36, graduated from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) in 2013

My item is … a 24-in stainless-steel Staedtler ruler with nonslip cork backing and engraved tick marks (from the 963 series).

It was a bit of a splurge for a college freshman and some of the cork has peeled away, but the ruler has otherwise held up remarkably well over nearly two decades. It’s still as straight as an arrow and I’m still as detail-obsessed as the day that I bought it.

I’m fairly certain I bought it in Albany at Arlene’s Artist Materials, a one-stop shop for design students and creatives all over the New York Capital District. (I never met the titular Arlene – as a young adult I never thought to ask if she was real – but let’s just say I owe “her” a lot for always having what I needed, when I needed it.) Not surprisingly I do a lot less model-making and drafting by hand these days, but the ruler comes in handy for the many projects that seem to constantly litter my small Brooklyn apartment. The extra length is great for retrieving objects that my cat has swatted into hard-to-reach nooks too.

Angela Serratore, 40, graduated from a master’s program at Columbia in 2013

My item is … a painted wire shoe rack from Urban Outfitters that is now extinct.

I bought it when I moved into what I genuinely think might have been the smallest studio apartment on the Upper West Side. I had this idea that all of my storage pieces had to also be “cute,” so I got this rack that we then would have called twee and now would describe as “Pioneer Woman-esque,” in that it looks like it came from a 1930s farmhouse kitchen, but is obviously not an actual vintage piece. During my time in that apartment I used it for both shoes and mail, and when I moved into a series of larger spaces with closets it became a shoe rack. It’s actually not a great shoe rack – not enough space to spread the shoes out, sort of clunky, heels get stuck in the wire shelves – but I can’t bring myself to part with it! I still think it’s cute and it is also very sturdy – maybe I will repurpose it once again and use it in the kitchen!

Seymen Usta, 38, graduated from Karadeniz Technical University in 2011

My item is … an over-the-door shoe organizer I bought for $8.99 my freshman year of college.

I would not say the bag is special … However, in terms of sentimental value, it is unique. It has survived three different apartments and a house, only to be used as a brief storage for shoes in the first and has ended up as the least likely storage solution for my garage. The pockets are stretched out, some are torn, and it’s permanently stained with old oil-based enamel that will not come off. The hooks are bent and broken over the years from struggling to hang on many doors.

There is something oddly satisfying in the thought that a small bag with torn pockets is the most appropriate tool for holding my garage supplies and tools. Every time I reach for the can of Rust-Oleum in the bag, I am greeted with a wave of nostalgia that hits me with the thought that in 2006, the biggest problem in my life was fitting six pairs of shoes into a dorm closet.

David Zhong, 28, graduated from Douglas college in 2019

My item is … a basic plastic shower caddy.

The one piece of dorm gear I bought at UBC that has outlived everything else is a basic plastic shower caddy I purchased more than a decade ago. As a student, I would toss my shampoo and body wash in the container on my way down the residence hallway to the showers. Today, the same caddy holds chalk blocks, resistance bands and stopwatch timers in my commercial training facility, between client sessions.

When I was building my kinesiology practice, I had to make many sacrifices on the path to establishing my business. My first commercial-grade training facility didn’t have the budget for nice equipment, so I brought in my old caddy as a utility storage bin. I needed something portable and easy to clean to transport mobility tools around the weight room floor between client sessions. This seemingly unimpressive piece of plastic has outlived four facility relocations and thousands of client workouts.

Finbarre Snarey, 48, graduated from Manchester Metropolitan University in 1999

My item is … a beloved carved wooden box that I used to keep my Rider-Waite-Smith tarot cards in at university.

I bought it from Birmingham’s Bull Ring market in the mid 1990s. It was probably intended as a jewellery or keepsake box, but it was the perfect size for a tarot deck. I bought it straight after seeing The Craft at the Odeon cinema. Eight house moves and three decades later, it is still where I keep them. The box still sits at home holding the same deck of cards. The wood and carving have little worn in places and these days I use the cards as prompts for inspiration.

I would only replace it if the lid came off, and even then I wouldn’t get rid of it. It has become part of the history of the cards I have kept inside. A modern equivalent might be this gorgeous hand-carved wooden keepsake box on Amazon, but a new one wouldn’t carry the same memories.

Ian Glennon, 57, graduated from University of Southampton in 2005

My item is … a collapsible bookshelf

I bought it in a furniture shop in Farnborough. It’s special because I’m a book addict and this bookshelf has come with me on my travels. Wherever I’ve lived, I always knew my books had a home. Of course, I have more bookshelves now (not enough!), but this one has pride of place next to my desk. At university it was home to my expanding sci-fi collection, many classics and my course textbooks. It also doubles up as a display cabinet.

It’s where I keep many of my “British books”, the ones that also followed me around the world in boxes and suitcases: Tolkien, Iain M Banks, Arthur C Clarke, JK Rowling and Conan Doyle among many others. They all have a home for life on this bookshelf. It’s the record of my reading life.

It’s been driven to Denmark from England, taken by lorry to Sweden and boated by cargo ship to the USA. I will pass it on in my will to one of my kids. I only hope that they actually have books to put on it!

Karen Yuan, 30, graduated from Columbia University in 2018

My item is … instant abalone porridge.

Ten years later, I still keep a few bags of this instant abalone porridge in my pantry as a little treat. In college, I discovered it while wandering H-Mart late at night – back when my life choices meant studying at ungodly hours and calling instant porridge “dinner.” Whenever I was stressed, sick or just too tired to function, I turned to this microwaveable comfort food that somehow tasted perfectly salted with a deep briny savor that made it feel like a hearty meal. These days I make my own congee in my Cuckoo rice cooker, but whenever I find myself back in Manhattan’s East Village H-Mart, you can spot me grabbing this off its shelf among the hoodie-wearing, sleep-deprived youth.

Nick Mokey, 40, graduated from Syracuse University in 2008

My item is … a 165-piece Craftsman mechanic’s tool kit

I felt very adult hauling this shiny chrome toolkit off to college, despite not knowing much more than how to change my oil at the time. Marinating in Syracuse road salt, my Pontiac Grand Prix would give me plenty of practice in the years ahead: sealing a leaky trunk lid, replacing rusty wheel bearings and fixing the cursed “fan resistor pack” that required me to sit upside down in the passenger seat with my head in the foot well to reach it under the dashboard, not once, not twice, but three times.

Two cars, one van, and six motorcycles later, it’s still the box I haul out to the driveway when something is on the fritz. I have more tools now, sure, but it turns out the perfect size to stow under a dorm bed is also just the perfect size. This modern equivalent is still the set I’d issue a DIY-curious college freshman hellbent on maintaining a string of relentlessly unreliable vehicles.

title: Universities Settled Over Allegedly Baseless Probes. They’re Not Expressing Regret.
summary:
Universities Settled Over Allegedly Baseless Probes. They’re Not Expressing Regret.
Ryan Quinn Fri, 08/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

Former Justice Department lawyers say investigations into Brown and Columbia over alleged antisemitism were politically motivated. But it’s unclear whether federal officials will investigate the whistleblowers’ letter.

Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
Allegations that the Trump administration’s antisemitism probes into Ivy League universities were legally baseless aren’t new. What is new this week is who’s making them.

Three former Justice Department attorneys, through their own lawyers, filed whistleblower allegations against their former employer: the federal government.

The 25-page document from the lead whistleblower says Justice attorneys were assigned to the Health and Human Services Department as part of Trump’s multi-agency antisemitism task force and then directed to find evidence of pervasive antisemitism at Brown, Columbia and Harvard Universities. But they said the evidence was insufficient and that federal officials—who had already cut off federal funding to the universities before the evidence was gathered—ignored their legal opinions and eventually settled with Brown and Columbia. A legal expert told Inside Higher Ed this week those settlements, and associated payouts, will likely stand despite the allegations.

The lead whistleblower alleges, for instance, that Daniel Shieh, the HHS Office for Civil Rights associate deputy director, said the “initial plan was for Harvard to be the first example, but when negotiations broke down, officials tried to make Columbia the example.” Shieh allegedly said that if Columbia didn’t settle, “nobody knows what is going to happen next. Maybe Brown.” He also said, according to the whistleblower, that there was “not a Title VI violation” at Brown, but “there’s no way we’re going to get a letter of no violation cleared.” (Title VI prohibits antisemitic discrimination at higher ed institutions that accept federal funding, such as student financial aid.)

The whistleblower said that instead of substantiating a violation at Brown, “witnesses, including a Jewish student leader, multiple rabbis, and faculty member from the medical school, described Brown’s consistent, proactive responses to any allegations of antisemitism.”

But Brown and Columbia settled with the Trump administration anyway last year, amid these investigations. Columbia gave up $221 million and Brown gave up $50 million; both surrendered some autonomy to the federal government in what faculty critics called capitulations that emboldened Trump officials.

Columbia’s commitments included providing the administration with admissions data, asking international student applicants “their reasons for wishing to study in the United States” and undertaking a “thorough review of the portfolio of programs in regional areas across the university, starting immediately with the Middle East.” Brown committed to adopt the Trump administration’s definitions of male and female and ban its doctors from prescribing puberty blockers to minors, among other provisions. Only Harvard fought back in court, and it’s won so far.

Asked by Inside Higher Ed whether they now regret entering into these settlements, or plan to find some way to exit them, Columbia declined to comment while a Brown spokesperson sent a long statement defending the agreement but not saying whether it seeks to exit it. Brown had faced $510 million in frozen federal research funds, with future funding also cut off.

This “posed enormous challenges for Brown’s research mission and financial sustainability, and if left unaddressed, would have undermined our ability to conduct life-saving research and to offer our students a world-class education,” the university’s statement said, adding that the settlement “permanently closed three open reviews of the University’s federal compliance with anti-discrimination laws” while restoring “medical and health sciences research funding” and preserving “the ability for our students and scholars to teach and learn without government intrusion.”

It’s unclear whether the universities could even escape the settlements, if they wished. The universities both denied wrongdoing, and the agreements don’t list any findings that the federal government may have made.

“Anything can be brought to court,” said Peter Lake, a Stetson University law professor. But he said getting out of these settlements would be “challenging, to say the least.”

“It’s not as if Brown and Columbia probably didn’t have instincts that this might have been going on anyway,” Lake said, even without the new whistleblower disclosure.

Catherine Lhamon, who led the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights during the Obama and Biden administrations, said the whistleblower allegations are an embarrassment for the Trump administration and for the civil rights laws she says it’s misusing.

But Lhamon, who’s now executive director of the University of California, Berkeley’s Edley Center on Law and Democracy, said she also hopes Brown and Columbia are “embarrassed about having compromised their students’ rights, their campus rights and the health of our democracy through the agreements they entered into.”

The whistleblower allegations themselves could lead to changes, but that requires officials to pay attention to them. Generally, they don’t have to.

Some Investigators Don’t Have to Investigate

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the House Judiciary Committee’s top Democrat, who published the whistleblower allegations, has launched an investigation, according to a news release this week.

“We’re heartened Congressman Raskin is obviously taking this very seriously,” said Dana Gold, senior director of advocacy and strategy with the Government Accountability Project and one of the lawyers representing the whistleblowers. But she noted that it’s not a bipartisan investigation, and the minority party doesn’t have subpoena power.

“It’s early days to see what level of interest we’ll get from other congressional committee staff,” Gold said.

The Government Accountability Project sent the whistleblower allegations to Republicans and Democrats on the House and Senate Judiciary Committees. The Republicans who chair both committees haven’t announced investigations.

A spokesperson for Chuck Grassley, the Iowa senator who chairs that chamber’s committee, told Inside Higher Ed in an email only that his “office is in receipt of this disclosure and will review the information.” A spokesperson for the House committee led by Jim Jordan, an Ohio Republican, said in an email that “there’s no denying that antisemitism on college campuses is a serious problem. The Committee strongly supports the Administration’s work to fight this hatred.”

But how Congress responds to the allegations could change next year, depending on whether the midterm elections change which party controls the House and Senate.

The Government Accountability Project also sent the allegations to the U.S. special counsel and the Justice and HHS inspectors general. Justice’s Office of the Inspector General didn’t respond to a call left by Inside Higher Ed, while a spokesperson for the HHS Office of the Inspector General said in an email that “we received the letter and are reviewing it for appropriate action.”

The Office of Special Counsel does have to look into this. Federal law says the special counsel must at least “determine whether there is a substantial likelihood” that the whistleblower information “discloses a violation of any law, rule, or regulation, or gross mismanagement, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority, or substantial and specific danger to public health and safety.” And the special counsel must do so within 45 days.

Gold said the Government Accountability Project should hear from that office about interviewing the whistleblowers. She said part of her organization’s goal “is to create opportunities for oversight entities to do their work of accountability and protecting the public interest and using evidence to comply with law.”

“When the most powerful law enforcement entity is abusing its authority to terrorize enemies, or towards political ends, we should all be very concerned when that much power can be weaponized,” Gold said, adding that “when the rule of law is turned into a weapon, as opposed to a tool for enforcement of laws on the books, then the threat to democracy is grave.”

The White House referred questions to Justice and HHS. HHS hasn’t responded to requests for comment, while Justice said in a statement, “The Department stands behind the integrity of these investigations.”

Allegations of Slanted Investigations

The lead whistleblower letter includes numerous specific allegations suggesting that the investigations weren’t motivated by actual evidence of pervasive antisemitism.

Shieh, the HHS official, allegedly said officials expanded probes that focused on medical schools to cover entire universities because “he did not think the facts surfaced through investigation to date would justify a finding of a Title VI violation at the medical schools.”

He also allegedly “explained a plan to systematically interview Middle East studies professors” at Brown, “particularly Muslim faculty,” noting an interview with one professor “was not ‘to get information’ but to see ‘what he will say.’” The whistleblower said she took that to mean trying to elicit a remark HHS could label antisemitic.

“The DOJ assignees repeatedly pushed back on having Middle East studies professors who were not connected to complaints of antisemitism on the witness interview list, but leadership refused to take them off,” the whistleblower letter says, adding that leaders didn’t pursue suggestions to also investigate allegations of anti-Muslim bias on campuses.

The lead whistleblower further says Justice lawyers were given just an hour to read the legal section regarding findings that Columbia had violated Title VI. At one point, Shieh allegedly said in “at least a moment of pause” that “it can’t be right that billions of dollars can be pulled for anything.”

Shieh also allegedly “acknowledged that the team had done a good job convincing the front office that they should move on from Brown, but unspecified ‘stakeholders’ had ‘approached the Task Force’ demanding action” and “informed the team that those stakeholders also wanted to open a compliance review into Northwestern.” (Northwestern University, which isn’t mentioned elsewhere in the whistleblower letter, eventually settled with the Trump administration, as did Cornell University.)

Members of the Columbia chapter of the American Association of University Professors are calling the whistleblower allegations “vindication.” The national AAUP and the American Federation of Teachers sued on behalf of their Columbia members over the funding freeze, but a judge dismissed the case because she said only the university had standing to sue.

“We knew that the legal process for rescinding grants wasn’t being fulfilled,” said Page Fortna, the chapter president. Nevertheless, she said she’s surprised by how “flimsy” the evidence of Title VI violations was, according to the whistleblowers. She said the complaint undermines the legitimacy of both the university’s general counsel and the Board of Trustees.

Rob Newton, the AAUP chapter’s secretary, said, “I would be surprised if this agreement is enforceable, given the way that we now know it was arranged on the side of the federal government. This is essentially a blackmail operation.”

title: An Earn-While-You-Learn Path Into Teaching
summary:
An Earn-While-You-Learn Path Into Teaching
Joshua.Bay Fri, 08/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

A report from New America finds teacher degree apprenticeships could lower barriers to the profession for working adults and nontraditional students.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
As a new academic year begins, teacher shortages remain a challenge for K–12 districts nationwide. Addressing those workforce needs will require long-term strategies, including building new pathways into the profession, researchers say.

A new report from New America’s Center on Education & Labor examines one such pathway: teacher degree apprenticeships. These programs allow aspiring educators to earn a paycheck while completing their degree and teaching certification.

Amaya Garcia, director of Pre-K–12 research and practice at New America, said the earn-while-you-learn model can make the profession more accessible for aspiring teachers who face financial barriers, particularly working adults and other nontraditional students.

“One thing we hear consistently is this idea that people don’t want to become teachers, and I think that statement is a little bit misleading,” Garcia said. “There are people who are in our communities and who are working in schools who do want to become teachers, but they face barriers, and some of these barriers include financial barriers.”

Who apprenticeships reach: Teacher degree apprenticeships have expanded rapidly in recent years. As of summer 2025, New America identified 157 programs across 44 states and Washington, D.C.

According to the most recent data from the U.S. Department of Labor, there are 6,275 active K–12 teacher apprentices nationwide.

The apprentices also look different from both the traditional college student and the existing teacher workforce. Three-quarters are between the ages of 25 and 54, and around two-thirds have not yet earned a bachelor’s degree.

Teacher apprentices are also more racially and ethnically diverse than the K–12 teacher workforce. Some 18 percent of apprentices identify as Black and 19 percent as Latino, compared with 6 percent and 9 percent of K–12 teachers, respectively.

Garcia said the findings suggest teacher degree apprenticeships could help narrow the demographic mismatch between students and teachers while expanding access to the profession for groups historically underrepresented in teaching. The programs can also provide a pathway for paraprofessionals and other school-based staff who already have experience working with students but lack teaching certification.

“Paraprofessionals, oftentimes, their demographics are closely similar to student demographics, so you’re hitting a lot of birds with one stone in a way,” Garcia said.

For working adults and other nontraditional students, Garcia said apprenticeships can also be structured to address barriers outside the classroom that can make completing a degree more difficult.

“People have to take care of their kids, so some of these programs have found ways to provide help towards things like childcare, transportation and other kinds of costs that come up along the way,” Garcia said.

Earn-while-you-learn models: The new analysis builds on earlier New America research examining the broader degree-apprenticeship landscape, which found access to such programs remains limited and uneven.

That study found that about 350 institutions nationwide offered nearly 600 apprenticeship programs integrated with associate, bachelor’s or master’s degrees, preparing students for 91 occupations. About one-third of the programs were in education, with teaching the most common occupation represented.

Garcia said much of the growth in teacher degree apprenticeships occurred during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, aided by temporary federal investments, including State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds and Department of Labor apprenticeship grants.

But as those funding sources expire, programs are increasingly looking for more long-term ways to cover the costs of earning a degree and teaching credentials.

“They’re sort of shifting that approach because they realize that it’s not sustainable,” Garcia said.

She said some programs are combining funding sources, including Pell Grants for eligible apprentices, to reduce how much students pay out of pocket. Programs can also award credit for prior learning, allowing apprentices to receive academic credit for skills and experience they already have and potentially reducing the time and cost required to complete a degree.

“There’s these different connection points happening to make sure that the costs are coming and are being paid for by more than just the student,” Garcia said. “They are trying to minimize that financial cost as much as they can by being creative about the different ways that they fund things.”

Learning by doing: Garcia said teacher degree apprenticeships ultimately offer colleges and school districts an opportunity to rethink how aspiring teachers are prepared by more closely connecting coursework with their experiences in the classroom.

“Traditional teacher prep gets a lot of flak for being too theoretical,” Garcia said. “So this is an opportunity for them to actually work closely with the district and say, ‘What are the things that your students are experiencing in the classrooms that they’re working in, and how do we align our curriculum?’”

One area that needs more attention and research, Garcia noted, is mentorship for teacher degree apprentices.

“Part of what these programs hinge on is that you’re going to be paired with a mentor teacher who’s going to help you learn skills and competencies that are going to help you become better prepared for the job,” Garcia said. “Being a mentor teacher to an apprentice is very different from being a supervising teacher to a student teacher.”

That distinction makes how programs select mentors and pair them with apprentices particularly important, Garcia said, including whether candidates benefit from mentors who share similar backgrounds or characteristics.

Despite the clear benefits of teacher apprentices, Garcia said colleges and districts need to think more intentionally about how to integrate the model into existing teacher-preparation systems.

“There is a lot of opportunity there, but it’s just not something that we’ve traditionally done in teacher preparation,” Garcia said. “So really thinking about how you take advantage of what apprenticeships have to offer and mapping it onto teacher preparation—I think there’s still some work to be done.”

title: University Suspends Academic Who Accused Jason Arday of Plagiarism

University Suspends Academic Who Accused Jason Arday of Plagiarism

Seher Asaf for Times Higher Education
full_text:
Belgium’s Ghent University has suspended Nathan Cofnas, the controversial scholar whose blog accusing Jason Arday of plagiarism led to widespread public scrutiny of the late University of Cambridge professor’s academic record and personal achievements.

Ghent said in a statement that it has launched “a preliminary disciplinary investigation” into Cofnas, a postdoctoral researcher in its Department of Philosophy and Moral Sciences.

“As part of this process, the university is assessing whether there are sufficient grounds to refer the case to the competent disciplinary body for further consideration,” it said.

“Pending this preliminary investigation, Ghent University has suspended the staff member as a precautionary measure. The university cannot comment further on the specific details of the disciplinary case or the underlying arguments, in order to safeguard the confidentiality of the personnel file and the disciplinary proceedings.”

Last month Cofnas, a self-described “race realist,” accused Arday of plagiarizing parts of his Ph.D. thesis at Liverpool John Moores University.

Arday resigned from Cambridge on Aug. 5. He denied the plagiarism allegations but acknowledged errors in his work. Liverpool John Moores investigated and concluded that his Ph.D. should stand.

Last week the former sociology professor was found dead in London. The cause of his death is unknown. Police have said it is being treated as unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.

Cofnas acknowledged on X that he had been suspended by the university. “They will almost certainly fire me,” he said. “The decision was made by rector Petra De Sutter, a former leader of the Green Party.”

The suspension comes after Ghent said that following Arday’s death it had “received many enquiries” about Cofnas’s appointment.

“We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited. It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others,” Ghent said in its statement.

“For this reason, the university takes the recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously. Ghent University has decided to take appropriate action within its powers and the applicable framework.”

In March, more than 300 staff and students wrote an open letter to the university, questioning the appointment of Cofnas and accusing Ghent of violating its code of conduct.

At the time, the university defended the decision, saying that Cofnas “was selected as the most suitable candidate following a procedurally correct and duly conducted selection process.”

title: Some Students Can Now Venmo Their College Tuition
summary:
Some Students Can Now Venmo Their College Tuition
Johanna Alonso Fri, 08/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

A massive portion of Gen Z uses money-transfer apps like Venmo every day, so allowing students to use them to pay their tuition was a natural step, the company said.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Students at some U.S. universities are now able to pay their tuition through Venmo or its parent company, PayPal, the financial technology giant announced Wednesday.

PayPal has partnered with three top tuition-payment companies, which collectively service over a thousand universities, to allow students to pay tuition and fees through PayPal and Venmo, according to the announcement. Students at a handful of institutions, like Michigan State University and Texas Tech University, can already use those platforms to pay their institutions, and PayPal said it expects more to join in the coming year.

The goal of these partnerships, the company stated, is to make paying tuition more convenient for students, many of whom already use money-transfer apps like PayPal and Venmo in their daily lives.

“Students and families want the flexibility to use payment methods that fit how they manage their money, while institutions need those options to work within the systems and processes their teams already rely on,” Don Smith, senior vice president and general manager of integrated payments at Illumia, one of the education-payment platforms PayPal is working with, said in the announcement. “This integration helps schools expand choice in a practical way, improving the payer experience without creating a disconnected path for campus teams.”

To pay this way, students will go to their institutions’ regular payment portals, where they will be given the option to pay via PayPal or Venmo, among regular card options.

This isn’t the company’s first foray into higher education. PayPal already has agreements with the Big Ten and Big 12 athletic conferences to allow institutions to make revenue-sharing payments to athletes via Venmo.

Bryan Dickson, director of education policy at the National Association of College and University Business Officers, said this feels like a natural progression for how colleges handle tuition payments, following the transition from paper checks to electronic payments.

“Institutions want to meet the demand of the market. Just as we’ve seen institutions adjust to the needs of the students when it comes to housing, dining, activities and campus services—PayPal, Venmo and other tools are fairly ubiquitous these days,” he said.

But Mike Pierce, executive director and co-founder of Protect Borrowers, a nonprofit dedicated to fighting predatory lending, said he was concerned about the offering in light of evidence from a 2020 report that some unaccredited, for-profit workforce-training programs advertised PayPal Credit as a way for their students to pay tuition.

At the time, PayPal said it had no formal relationship with those for-profit schools and did not advertise to that sector. Following the report, the company disallowed programs that were using misleading language to use PayPal Credit.

“I think that advocates for students should be skeptical of these kinds of deals, because faster and simpler payment processing isn’t really the thing holding people back from going to college; it’s not having enough money,” Pierce said. “When you have massive companies getting into the student payment scheme … we should be skeptical.”

In an email to Inside Higher Ed, PayPal said students will not be able to apply for PayPal Credit or Buy Now, Pay Later loans when paying their tuition; instead, they can use their balances on those apps, or cards or bank accounts connected to their accounts. The universities will pay transaction fees to PayPal.

“For Gen Z, digital-first payment behavior is the norm. Students already use PayPal and Venmo for rent, for splitting a bill and for paying friends and family back. Now that same experience shows up as a payment option for tuition too, right at checkout,” the company wrote, citing a forthcoming report in which 94 percent of Gen Z survey respondents said they use a payment app weekly. “Parents value that same security. Many have used PayPal for decades, and tuition is one of the largest payments a family makes. Being able to pay it through a network they already trust, with the ease and flexibility they expect, makes a payment of this size feel less daunting.”

title: Berkeley Report Says Trusting Campus Climate ‘Vital’ to University’s Mission
summary:
Berkeley Report Says Trusting Campus Climate ‘Vital’ to University’s Mission
Emma Whitford Fri, 08/21/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
A faculty task force at the University of California, Berkeley, determined that—in addition to policies protecting free speech and academic freedom—a campus climate “characterized by trust and good faith” is essential to achieving the university’s core mission, according to a report released Thursday.

The task force convened a year ago to examine “whether existing policies and conceptual frameworks in higher education are sufficient to address the emerging dilemmas at UC Berkeley or if new approaches are needed for the changing political context,” the report states. Berkeley has seen its fair share of recent political controversies. In just the past year, the university was at the center of an investigation into alleged antisemitism on campus, student protesters were charged with vandalism, a lecturer was suspended for making pro-Palestine comments during class and the university removed political artwork from the Multicultural Community Center, among other events.

An ideal campus climate is one in which students and employees have “confidence that each member of the campus community will follow through with what they have agreed to do and/or what is expected of them, that they will advance the collective interests of the university, and that they will treat others with dignity, honesty, and fairness even in the face of disagreement,” the report states. This is important because the formal rules that protect academic freedom “may do little work in practice” if faculty members are not confident that administrators will protect them, the task force argues. The same is true for students relying on officials to apply free speech policies equally.

Going forward, the task force urged Berkeley officials to be candid about why they make specific judgment calls about political speech on campus. They also suggest that the university issue statements emphasizing its values and policies “when invited speakers make incendiary and derogatory claims about members of the campus community.”

“Policy documents focused on free speech often demand civility and respect from members of the campus community when controversial speakers are invited to campuses. But speakers themselves do not always adhere to the norms of civility and respect,” the task force wrote.

In a statement, the campus administration said they appreciate the task force's interest in free speech, academic freedom and campus climate issues and "look forward to continued collaboration" with the Academic Senate.

"UC Berkeley doesn’t just support Free Speech and engagement with the issues of the day, we encourage it," administrators wrote. "When speaking for themselves, members of our community have every right to have their voices heard in support of the causes they believe in, and so this campus must and always will take a viewpoint-neutral approach when it comes to supporting freedom of speech and academic freedom."

(12:30 p.m. Aug. 21: Updated to add a statement from the university.)

title: Jason Arday and the new politics of plagiarism
summary: The resignation and death of the Cambridge professor is the latest chapter in a centuries-old struggle over originality and intellectual ownership – one intensified by the rise of generative AI.
full_text:
After a meteoric rise to the top ranks of British academia, scholar Jason Arday was found dead at his London home on Aug. 14, 2026.

Arday had spent weeks fighting plagiarism accusations. The way they took on a life of their own in the media ecosystem is a stark reminder of the steep price people can pay in a culture that has made originality a kind of moral virtue.

In 2023, at age 38, he had been appointed to a professorship in sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the youngest Black professor in the institution’s 800-year history.

Nine days before his death, Arday had resigned from his faculty position. He was facing growing criticism about improbable and inconsistent details appearing in his memoir, scheduled to be released in the coming weeks by Simon & Schuster. Arday’s publisher had stood by him, lauding the academic’s “professionalism and integrity.”

But the originality of Arday’s dissertation and his other academic work was also coming under scrutiny, leading to multiple allegations of plagiarism.

Arday vehemently denied the accusations, suggesting that any mistakes were the result of his autism. He also claimed that his accusers were motivated by racism.

The controversy over Arday’s work reflects an ongoing trend of ideological opponents levying plagiarism accusations to undermine one another. I think it’s also worth exploring why such attacks continue to be so enticing – and so effective.

Shifting standards for originality

Plagiarism can be defined as the appropriation of someone else’s words or ideas without acknowledgment or compensation.

In the ancient world, plagiarism was viewed quite negatively: The word “plagiarism” actually means “kidnapper” in Latin, and the Roman poet Horace described literary theft like a crow making itself beautiful with stolen feathers.

But in my 2026 book, “Strikingly Similar,” I explore how, throughout the medieval period, the Renaissance and into the early modern era, an ethos of “imitatio” prevailed. Chaucer, Shakespeare and Milton are examples of authors who hewed closely to writers who had come before them. These writers freely borrowed plots, characters and rhetorical devices in the service of their own work.

True originality came to be viewed in a positive light only gradually, and it eventually developed into the modern concept of intellectual property, in which the creative products of human ingenuity are viewed as tangible assets. Treating creative works as property, in turn, created the legal framework to protect them.

The German artist Albrecht Dürer initiated one of the first known intellectual property lawsuits. In 1506, he asked the Venetian government to stop the Italian engraver Marcantonio Raimondi from copying his woodcuts. Dürer was only partly successful: It was decided that Raimondi could continue copying Dürer’s work, but he was prohibited from also copying the artist’s distinctive monogram.

In the 19th century, as the result of lobbying by authors such as Charles Dickens, the British Parliament enacted the Copyright Act of 1842. This statute greatly expanded the protections granted to authors. It would take another 50 years, however, before foreign authors like Dickens enjoyed similar protections under U.S. copyright law.

Today, the situation that existed during the Renaissance has almost totally reversed itself.

In Europe, groups of scholars have banded together to investigate allegations of plagiarism. Using crowdsourcing techniques, VroniPlag Wiki in Germany and Dissernet in Russia have exposed numerous instances of plagiarism by public servants in their dissertations and academic publications.

The work of VroniPlag Wiki alone has led to several German universities revoking doctoral degrees they had awarded to elected and appointed government officials.

Plagiarism becomes political

Today, accusations of plagiarism have become a potent way to undermine someone’s credibility. If a claim is substantiated, the plagiarist is seen as sloppy or lazy at best, and fundamentally dishonest at worst.

As a result, partisans of the political left and right routinely use allegations of plagiarism to vilify their ideological adversaries. This serves their goals of undercutting both their target’s work and the institutions they represent.

In 1991, NPR’s Nina Totenberg broke the story of Anita Hill’s allegations of sexual harassment against Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas, drawing the ire of the right. As the controversy engulfed the confirmation process, the conservative-leaning Wall Street Journal revived a nearly two-decade-old plagiarism accusation against Totenberg, dating from her time as a reporter for the National Observer.

The most prominent recent example would be the 2023 claim by conservative activist Christopher Rufo that Claudine Gay, then serving as president of Harvard, had engaged in multiple acts of plagiarism.

In 2024, Gay resigned as the school’s president, although she remains on the faculty. (In an ironic twist, the spouse of one of Gay’s most prominent critics, hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, was accused of having plagiarized her own dissertation.)

Conservative voices have also routinely found themselves in the crosshairs.

In 2013, multiple media outlets accused Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul of plagiarizing in his speeches, newspaper column and his 2012 book from a variety of sources, including Wikipedia. And during Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch’s 2017 confirmation hearings, some media outlets claimed that President Donald Trump’s nominee had plagiarized parts of his 2006 book about assisted suicide. Gorsuch went on to be confirmed by the Senate.

The accusations against Arday did not emerge in a political vacuum. They were shaped by the culture wars over race, academia and diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

On July 21, 2026, Nathan Cofnas, an American philosopher working at Ghent University in Belgium, wrote a Substack post detailing how he submitted Arday’s 2015 dissertation to Copyleaks, a plagiarism detection platform. He found “substantial overlap” with a thesis written by another scholar in 2009.

Cofnas added that “Many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source,” and found similar issues in other papers written by Arday.

In the past, Cofnas has expressed doubts about the intellectual abilities of Blacks in comparison to whites. By discrediting the work of a Black professor, he explained, he could also discredit the university that had hired Arday for promoting “the ideology of DEI.”

Ghent University suspended Cofnas on August 20, 2026, while it conducted an investigation into his actions.

AI complicates the notion of plagiarism

The rise of generative artificial intelligence has arguably made the public’s desire for original human works even more pronounced. Just a year after the 2022 release of ChatGPT 3.5, Merriam-Webster chose “authentic” as its word of the year.

Copyright laws also underscore the premium we place on originality by granting creators – and even their heirs – long periods of exclusive rights for books, music and other artistic works.

When a student submits a paper written by a chatbot instead of their own work, should this be considered plagiarism? I’ve argued that this is more akin to ghostwriting, since the student isn’t copying from an original source. Instead, generative AI is stringing words together in a probabilistic way that closely resembles human writing.

That isn’t the same as generating a text from a single source. That said, using a chatbot to write without disclosing its use can still be a form of cheating. And most people contend that plagiarism, cheating and ghostwriting are all cut from the same cloth because they all lack the spark that we ascribe to truly original thinking and writing.

The public ultimately expects journalists, scholars and elected officials to behave ethically. In academia, there is no greater sin than passing off another’s work as one’s own. And violations of public trust are typically judged quite harshly.

title: Gen Alpha protests mirror government report: Big gaps in school education
summary: Issues Neither Unique To Any Region, Nor Universal

Student protests highlight gaps in teachers, toilets and basic school infrastructure across India

NEW DELHI: Another kind of student protest is beginning to surface on social media - schoolchildren demanding small fixes: a teacher, a usable toilet, a playground, sometimes even a proper road to school. The complaints may be local, but data suggests the gaps they point to are widespread. In Hamirpur, 300 children marched 6km to the collectorate seeking a usable road to school; in Lucknow, 250 girls marched over teacher shortages and basic amenities; in Jaipur, students with disabilities protested over toilets, sanitation and unsafe classrooms. Jharkhand has 36 pupils per teacher, West Bengal has internet in only 19.7% of schools and Meghalaya has toilets for children with special needs in just 6.3%. Data shows uneven school infrastructure, with major gaps in internet, computers and accessibility.

State govts run 68.4% of India's schools and private unaided managements 23.3%. Of the country's 14,66,682 schools, 10,03,051 are state govt-run and 2,194 are central govt schools. title: Freedom of religion can’t override public order, societal norms: Patna HC
full_text:
Patna HC rules religious freedom is not absolute, says public health, safety and law & order must take precedence.

PATNA: The Patna high court, in a significant verdict, has ruled that the fundamental right to religious freedom guaranteed by the Constitution is not absolute and cannot override public law and order. The court said such right must be exercised in harmony with the rights of other people and societal norms. A single bench of justice Alok Kumar dismissed a writ petition filed by Bhadai Chaudhary on behalf of an “akhara” (monastery of a Hindu sect), holding that the state govt should give primacy to public health, safety and tranquility while granting permission for any religious procession (julus), particularly in a residential area. The verdict was passed and uploaded to the high court website on Thursday but came to public domain on Friday. Justice Kumar further observed, “Secularism is the basic structure of Indian Constitution and the fundamental right of religious freedom affecting general civic life and amenities has to undergo parameters of ‘reasonable restrictions’ provided in Constitution itself.” The writ petition sought a direction to the state govt to grant permission for 300 persons to hold the “Mahabiri Julus” (religious procession), conducted yearly on the 11th day of the Bhadra month (last Aug/first Sept fortnight) of the Vikram calendar by an “akhara” in Hathuara village of Siwan district. The petitioner claimed such permission was a matter of fundamental right. The state govt, however, submitted in its counter affidavit that previous such processions had involved the torching of a public vehicle and public nuisance caused by marching mobs. The high court found the issue covered by the Supreme Court’s verdict in the case of Dr M Ismail Faruqui, which held that offering prayers or worship, being a religious practice, is a matter of fundamental right. However, the location where such prayers or worship are offered stands on a different footing. The high court’s ruling, according to a legal expert, makes clear that while religious freedom is constitutionally protected, its exercise cannot be separated from considerations of public health, safety and tranquillity. “The court’s observations also underline the need to balance religious practices with the rights of others and the broader requirements of civic life, particularly when such activities are held in residential areas,” he said.

End of Article
