The truth is the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government has let Uttar Pradesh and country down by benefitting a selected few people, while allowing structural collapse of the education system,” said Afzal Ansari, Lok Sabha MP from Ghazipur and senior the Samajwadi Party (SP) leader.

Mr. Ansari said, “the protest be it Gen Alpha or Gen Z, points towards deeper anxiety and unrest in the society where young people are not provided employment opportunity by the system and government, the quality of education in government schools slipped due to lack of teachers and other fundamental loopholes like below standard teaching, hence students are angry with the system.”

“Rather than issuing checklist, the government need to initiate comprehensive reforms in the education sector to match international standards and provide scope of employability in future,” Mr. Ansari added.

Congress called the move of the checklist a ploy to divert attention from issues of school closure and below-standard teaching due to policy failure.

“In Uttar Pradesh, over 25,000 schools have been closed in the last nine years, the BJP government has completely failed in providing quality education, hence students are forced to hit the streets fighting for justice, such checklist are worthless if quality education is not imparted to students, I believe the BJP by design don’t want to impart quality education as the regime is fundamentally against logic, reasoning, they feel educate people will challenge its Hindutva centric authoritarian outlook,” said Anil Yadav, a senior Uttar Pradesh Congress leader.

The Uttar Pradesh Education Department, on August 20, issued a 14-point checklist to over 40,000 primary and secondary schools, including regular inspection of facilities such as drinking water, electricity supply, safety measures, blackboards, the quality of the mess, separate restrooms for boys and girls, and canteen food, among others. The government also directed officials to quickly check any complaint received through social media or other medium.

Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has stressed the need for comprehensive changes to ensure the systematic operation of state-run Jai Prakash Narayan Sarvodaya Schools. “Clear rules and regulations for the schools be prepared, the selection process for vacant teaching posts be expedited, and necessary action be taken towards the formation of a society so that the management and operation of these residential schools can be carried out more systematically,” said Mr. Adityanath while reviewing the Social Welfare department which runs these schools.

Jai Prakash Narayan Sarvodaya Schools, came under scanner after two large protests by students came in limelight over lack of teachers and quality of food served in these educational institutions.

title: America needs international students more than it thinks
summary:
International students are not simply beneficiaries of US higher education but vital contributors to its economy, communities and global competitiveness, says Bimpe Femi-Oyewo as she calls for a reframing of how they are viewed.

The post America needs international students more than it thinks appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
We need to stop talking about international students as though the United States is doing them a favour by letting them in.

It is not a one-way transaction.

International students contribute to the US economy, universities, local communities, research, innovation and the classroom. And increasingly, the data show just how much the US stands to lose as access becomes more difficult.

NAFSA’s Fall 2026 International Student Enrolment Outlook, published on August 11, “projects that the US could have as many as 111,000 fewer international students in fall 2026. The economic consequences are significant: up to $3.4bn in lost direct economic contributions and nearly 40,000 fewer jobs”.

These numbers should make policymakers pause.

Because behind every percentage point is a student who applied, was admitted, made plans, and hoped to begin a new chapter in the United States.

And many are not moving forward because they suddenly decided they do not want a US education. Barriers are stopping them.

Visa appointment bottlenecks. Processing delays. Travel restrictions. Changing immigration policies. Uncertainty around post-study opportunities. And, for students from countries facing bans or restrictions, the very real possibility that admission does not translate into the ability to enter the country.

NAFSA points to several of these factors as contributing to the projected decline. Its analysis notes “that international applications to US doctoral programs fell 21%, while international submissions through Common App fell 9%, including declines of 34% from Ghana and 17% from Nigeria”.

But the impact goes far beyond the numbers.

I know this personally. When I was a graduate student at Duke University, I used to joke that my program was a mini United Nations.

There were students from more than 20 countries, and it was the first time I had met people from places such as Kosovo or Kyrgyzstan.

That diversity was not a nice add-on. It was part of the education. We brought our experiences from different countries, industries, communities, and political and economic environments into the classroom. We challenged each other’s assumptions. We learned from one another. That is what makes international education so powerful, and that is what America risks losing.

International students bring revenue to universities and communities. They support jobs, they contribute to research and innovation, and they enrich classrooms. They create connections that extend far beyond graduation.

So when international students choose or are forced to look elsewhere, America loses too. This is why I believe we need to change the way we talk about international students.

The US gains from international students, and international students gain from the US, it has always been a two-way street.

They are not a burden to be managed and they are not simply people asking to be allowed into America. They are contributors and partners in a mutually beneficial relationship.

And the United States is not the only destination competing for their talent.

Students have choices. The UK, Canada, Australia, countries across Europe, and other emerging study destinations are actively seeking international talent. If one destination becomes increasingly difficult to navigate, students will eventually take their ambitions elsewhere.

Countries do not remain global education leaders simply because they once were, they remain leaders by continuing to attract the world’s talent.

That is why this conversation is bigger than international education.

It is about economic competitiveness. It is about innovation. It is about research. It is about the diversity of ideas that strengthens institutions.

And ultimately, it is about whether policy decisions are strengthening America’s global advantage or slowly giving it away.

I sincerely hope NAFSA’s projections serve as a wake-up call, because once students, researchers, and global talent decide to build their futures somewhere else, winning them back will not be easy.

The US gains from international students, and international students gain from the US, it has always been a two-way street.

Let’s stop pretending otherwise.

title: Five signals shaping European international education ahead of EAIE Glasgow 2026
summary:
From Erasmus reform and changing student flows to geopolitical uncertainty and the future of international partnerships, EAIE Glasgow arrives at a moment of recalibration for European higher education. Here are the issues likely to shape conversations on the ground.

The post Five signals shaping European international education ahead of EAIE Glasgow 2026 appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Europe is recalibrating its approach to international students

The Netherlands recently recorded its first-ever decline in international student numbers following policy measures designed to curb growth.

Elsewhere, governments and institutions are responding to the pressures created by international student growth, from housing and infrastructure constraints to tighter visa and compliance requirements.

At the same time, rising travel costs continue to create uncertainty for students planning to begin their studies this autumn.

The UK’s planned return to Erasmus+ from 2027 has also reignited debate about the future of student mobility. While the move has been broadly welcomed, many in the sector argue the next phase should combine the collaborative strengths of Erasmus+ with the global outlook and widening participation focus of the Turing Scheme.

Speaking to The PIE News, EAIE said that international student recruitment is increasingly being viewed through several lenses, including talent attraction, migration management and institutional resilience.

“Institutions are operating in a more politically sensitive environment shaped by employability concerns, housing pressure, and immigration debates,” said Jody Hoekstra-Selten, manager of knowledge development at EAIE.

Laura Rumbley, EAIE’s director for knowledge development and research, pointed to developments outside Europe as another factor reshaping the landscape. Political and policy upheaval in the major “big four” destination countries, she said, is “reframing the landscape of interests and possibilities” for internationally mobile students.

European institutions are consequently seeing themselves more clearly as “active players in an increasingly multipolar picture” for global student recruitment and mobility, she added.

Competition for global talent is intensifying

France has stepped up efforts to position itself as a destination for international researchers, recognising the opportunities created by changing geopolitical dynamics and increasing global competition for academic talent.

Germany, meanwhile, continues to demonstrate the value of connecting education with employment outcomes, with international graduates significantly more likely to find work after completing their studies.

“​​Attracting and retaining international talent could potentially become as important as recruiting students,” said Hoekstra-Selten.

Demographic decline and skills shortages are affecting countries across Europe, she added, while broader EU initiatives are seeking to make Europe a destination of choice for scientific and professional talent.

But making that ambition work will require more than recruitment, she said, warning that “pathways will need to be developed and put in place”.

Partnerships are becoming a bigger part of the internationalisation mix

As international enrolment becomes harder to predict, universities are looking beyond traditional student recruitment to build their global reach.

The UK’s transnational education activity is a good example: TNE exports grew 17% in 2024, reaching £3.6bn, even as growth in overall education exports slowed. Meanwhile, the number of students studying for UK university qualifications offshore is increasingly approaching the number of international students studying in the UK.

Across Europe, university alliances are taking international partnerships beyond traditional exchange agreements, with institutions exploring joint degrees, collaborative teaching, research and new forms of mobility.

EAIE is seeing a similar shift, with European institutions increasingly prioritising “deeper, longer-term partnerships over traditional exchange agreements”, said Hoekstra-Selten.

The range of purposes is also expanding, she added, with institutions looking to partnerships for student mobility, research collaboration, curriculum development, transnational education and innovation.

“The shift seems to be driven by funding opportunities, geopolitical uncertainty, and a desire to create more sustainable and measurable international engagement,” she said.

Rumbley also highlighted a broader shift in how European institutions engage with partners beyond Europe, including in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Southern Mediterranean.

European institutions have “much to share with the world, but also much to learn from international counterparts”, she said, with partners increasingly insisting on mutual benefit as the starting point for collaboration.

The cost of studying in Europe is rising

Affordability has long been one of Europe’s advantages in the global international student market, but that proposition is coming under pressure.

France has raised the minimum funds international students must demonstrate for a study visa by 43%, while non-EU tuition fees have also increased.

In Flanders, several universities are hiking fees for non-EU students after the government announced it would only subsidise 2% of non-EU enrolments. At the same time, international students face stricter visa scrutiny and tighter requirements for renewing residence permits from next year.

For institutions, the challenge is increasingly about balancing financial pressures with the need to remain attractive to international students.

Higher fees and proof-of-funds requirements are part of a wider affordability challenge, Hoekstra-Selten said, alongside housing shortages and rising living costs.

“Europe’s reputation for quality education remains strong,” she said, but institutions increasingly need to demonstrate that they understand students’ financial concerns and are prepared to support them through measures such as scholarships, housing support and clear communication around return on investment.

“Accessibility and competitiveness are important keywords at this moment in time,” she said.

Rumbley stressed that there is no single European experience when it comes to affordability, with study and living costs varying significantly between and within countries.

“Higher education institutions situated in less expensive contexts have a compelling message to share in this regard, while any institution featuring strong academic programming and positive graduate outcomes has a powerful argument for return on investment,” she said.

“Larger scale economic trends may not be things the higher education sector can control, but there are meaningful ways institutions can play to their strengths and tell their unique story of adding value to students’ educational and professional journeys,” added Rumbley.

The global recruitment map is being redrawn

Europe continues to view Asia as a priority region for student recruitment, research collaboration and institutional partnerships. But universities are facing growing competition from within the region itself, as destinations across Asia invest heavily in higher education and internationalisation strategies.

Institutions in the UK and Ireland are also being urged to rethink established approaches to markets such as Southeast Asia and India, as student expectations become increasingly focused on outcomes.

Rather than assuming traditional recruitment patterns will continue, European universities are having to diversify their markets and think harder about what differentiates their offer.

For European institutions, differentiation will be increasingly important, according to Hoekstra-Selten — and not simply through rankings.

“As alternative study destinations in Asia and elsewhere become increasingly attractive, students are looking for strong employability prospects, welcoming communities, affordable study options, international networks and opportunities for mobility across multiple countries,” she said.

Europe’s strengths, she added, include the diversity of its higher education systems, research excellence, multilingual environment and growing network of cross-border alliances.

Rumbley said it is vital for Europe’s diverse higher education systems and institutions to “remain open to international engagement and to continually evolve” as the global landscape changes.

The next edition of the EAIE Barometer, which tracks the experiences, priorities and challenges of internationalisation professionals across Europe, is due to be released on September 7 – with Rumbley encouraging “every international education professional working in Europe to fill it in”.

title: Sponsored: When migration becomes the product, education loses its value
summary:
The international education sector is navigating one of its most significant periods of change in recent years. As policies evolve and student priorities shift, this is an opportunity to be honest about how we communicate the value of studying abroad and, more importantly, how we prepare students for long-term success.

The post Sponsored: When migration becomes the product, education loses its value appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For years, immigration policy has moved steadily from the background of the international education conversation to its centre. Students understandably want to know what opportunities exist after graduation. In responding to that demand, however, the sector has increasingly placed post-study work opportunities at the heart of its messaging. Institutions have highlighted graduate work rights, agents have compared destinations by visa pathways, and, over time, immigration policy has become a defining factor in how many students evaluate where to study.

That is what it means for migration to become the product. It rarely happens through bad intent. But somewhere between answering students’ questions and building the pitch around them, the visa became the product and education became the packaging. When that happens, education loses its value: not in reality, but in the story, we talk about it.

That distinction matters because immigration policies are designed to change. They respond to economic priorities, labour market needs, and political realities. Education, on the other hand, is a long-term investment whose value should extend well beyond any single immigration policy. A value proposition built on a visa can be repriced by a single policy paper.

Recent changes in the UK illustrate this clearly. Tighter student visa rules, the removal of dependant eligibility for most taught master’s students, and the confirmed reduction of the Graduate Route from two years to eighteen months from January 2027 have reshaped how many prospective students assess the UK. For any institution whose recruitment message led with post-study work, this is what a product recall looks like. The result is uncertainty for students and new challenges for institutions operating in an increasingly competitive global market.

Somewhere between answering students’ questions and building the pitch around them, the visa became the product and education became the packaging

The changing employment landscape provides a timely reminder. In July 2025, the British Medical Association reported that 52% of doctors completing foundation training had not secured employment for the following month, with more than 30,000 applicants competing for around 10,000 specialty training places. Since then, the UK government has moved to prioritise UK medical graduates for training places. Medicine is simply the sharpest example of a wider truth the sector has been slow to say out loud: a visa can put a graduate into a labour market, but it cannot make the labour market want them.

These developments do not diminish the value of studying medicine in the UK. Instead, they reinforce why students increasingly need guidance that extends beyond admissions and visas. Career planning, labour market realities, and long-term employability have become just as important as choosing the right university or programme.

The wider sector is experiencing similar change. The Office for Students projects that around 45% of English higher education providers could face a deficit in 2025/26 as institutions adapt to changing patterns in international recruitment. This is what over-reliance looks like: institutions that recruited on the strength of migration terms are discovering that their revenue now moves with the Home Office. Financial resilience will come from recruitment strategies rooted in long-term student success rather than short-term enrolment cycles.

Too often, international student recruitment focuses on courses, rankings, destinations, and intakes, while far less attention is given to what happens after graduation. The sector measures its success at enrolment; students measure theirs at employment. The gap between those two measures is where trust is won or lost.

The outcomes data shows how real that gap has become. According to UKCISA’s analysis of the latest HESA Graduate Outcomes data, the proportion of employed international graduates working in highly skilled roles fell from 74% to 64% within a year. The Home Office’s own Graduate Route evaluation found that two-thirds of working Graduate Route users earned under £30,000 a year. These are the numbers behind the brochure, and prospective students increasingly find them before we share them.

These figures should not discourage students from studying abroad. Rather, they underline the importance of setting realistic expectations and ensuring that students are equipped with the skills, career support, and professional networks needed to succeed after graduation. A visa may create opportunity, but it cannot guarantee a career.

We have had to ask ourselves the question this piece asks of everyone else: does our counselling lead with education, or with immigration

This is where the sector, recruiters included, must hold itself to a higher standard. As an organisation that recruits students, we have had to ask ourselves the question this piece asks of everyone else: does our counselling lead with education, or with immigration? The most valuable thing any of us can offer is personalised, evidence-based guidance from the very beginning. A degree abroad is not the right choice for every student, and helping individuals determine whether it aligns with their ambitions is not a weakness; it is responsible guidance. In the long run, it is also better business than selling a pathway that policy can close overnight.

That means investing more intentionally in career guidance, stronger partnerships between universities and employers, clearer communication around graduate outcomes, and a more holistic approach to student success.

Migration policies have changed before and will change again. The value of education should not, and it will not, provided we stop treating the visa as the product. If the international education sector places learning, employability, and long-term impact at the centre of its value proposition, it will remain compelling through every policy cycle, because the lasting opportunities education creates for students, institutions, and society are the one part of the offer no government can revoke.

About the author: Oyinkansola Shobiye is a marketing associate at Study Now, where she implements marketing strategies and communications that support international student recruitment across the UK and Europe. She has experience in international education marketing, strategic communications, brand storytelling, campaign development, and partnership marketing. Her work focuses on helping prospective students make informed study abroad decisions through research-led marketing and strategic communication.

title: Retention Is Emotional, Not Just Academic: Practical Strategies That Keep Online Students Engaged
summary:
According to the U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics (2025), the percent of students enrolled in distance education courses in postsecondary institutions in the fall of 2024 was 53.8%. Importantly and unfortunately, the withdrawal rate for this population far outpaces traditional students attending higher education institutions, requiring a closer examination of factors that can be addressed to improve retention in this population. In a comprehensive study reporting post-pandemic online course […]

The post Retention Is Emotional, Not Just Academic: Practical Strategies That Keep Online Students Engaged  appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
According to the U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics (2025), the percent of students enrolled in distance education courses in postsecondary institutions in the fall of 2024 was 53.8%. Importantly and unfortunately, the withdrawal rate for this population far outpaces traditional students attending higher education institutions, requiring a closer examination of factors that can be addressed to improve retention in this population. In a comprehensive study reporting post-pandemic online course discontinuation, students reported withdrawing due to the following five undermining elements: misalignment between suitability of content and online content presentation, inexpertly prepared and/or unstimulating instruction, inadequate digital skills, insufficient institutional support and personal resources, and distracting environmental factors (Kaisara 2024).

Translated, this means online students who withdraw rarely do so because they cannot intellectually complete the work; instead, they drop out because they feel a disconnect between content and content presentation. They give up attending school because they are anxious about needing a computer, not just a phone, for learning. They do not persist at the higher education level because they feel uncertain and lack confidence regarding classroom navigation. Our digital learners’ retention rates are lower because they feel isolated online and feel poorly supported by the institution. Such students also withdraw because they feel ashamed of their poor digital skills. If so many of the root reasons our distance education students have for leaving are emotional, solutions to these barriers should also be emotional.

Using Predictability to Reduce Anxiety

A key emotional state that surfaces when considering online higher ed students is anxiety. Data from the Center for Collegiate Mental Health (CCMH) 2024 Annual Report indicates that anxiety remains one of the most prevalent and persistent mental health challenges faced by college students (Center for Collegiate Mental Health 2025). While this data point suggests anxiety is common among all higher education students, anxiety in online college students is even more prevalent than in traditional face-to-face college students (Li et al. 2024; Hayat et al. 2024). To mitigate the challenge posed by anxiety, an optimized and orderly online learning environment will aid in addressing predictability for students, ultimately leading to reduced anxiety, relief of uncertainty, and maximized accessibility.

As an online instructor for 20 years, I can attest to the power of predictable course rhythms. With uncertainty better managed, students know what to expect. Knowing what to expect reduces anxiety and the emotional cost of staying, hence retention grows. To encourage such retention, consider the following consistent course design choices and predictable instructional practices to systematize your classroom while enhancing its navigability:

Folder Feng Shui – Employ consistent naming conventions in online classrooms to streamline location and access and address unpredictability

No-dust Grading – Supply timely feedback with a 1-4 day turnaround time to reduce uneasiness

Prominent Prompting – Post predictable gentle reminders and announcements to reinforce engagement and instructor approachability

KISS – Keep It Short, Silly – Record chunked (five minutes or less) tutorials and weekly overviews to model expectations, connections between content and career relevance, and navigational components, effectively minimizing confusion

Using Vulnerability to Reduce Shame

Regulating anxiety due to unpredictability in the online classroom can be very effective, and reducing the shame experienced by many of our students due to the barriers complicating their return to school is equally important. To do so, instructors can calibrate their classroom interactions to capitalize on practices that emphasize vulnerability, revision, and growth as being inherent to success. Carol Dweck’s philosophy of growth mindset comes to mind when striving to address such concerns. According to Dweck (2007), as instructors, we must encourage the mindset of not yet. Students must be encouraged in a way that presents stumbling points or imperfections as temporary blocks that have not yet been circumvented—but can be overcome with further dedication and work.

Communications in announcements, feedback, and discussions should promote energy consistent with the message that struggling is developmental, not indicative of a deficit in character. If instructors can engage with students in a way that promotes revision as being intrinsic to the learning process, this can keep students from withdrawing after setbacks (Kim et al. 2022). Furthermore, promoting a student-instructor partnership mentality can improve student retention (Loes et al. 2024).

Likewise, being mindful of approachability, accessibility, outreach incentivizing, tone, and level of instructional organization can also play strong roles in improving satisfaction between instructors and student retention (Loes et al. 2024). To encourage vulnerability and positive relationships with students, I embrace the following practices that display my own vulnerability as an instructor:

Embrace the Ums – When recording, be vulnerable by using a headshot and speak unscripted – A few ums humanize instructors

Cheer and Nudge Communications – Send out short reminders congratulating or nudging students on mid-week task completion to encourage positive relationships

Balancing the Mess with the Magic – In feedback, comment conversationally, specifically, and holistically on strengths and areas for opportunity for all assignments to encourage growth

Master Modeling – Develop routine sample assignments and templates to reduce cognitive load and self-doubt

Extend Empathy – When students ask for an extension or share a difficulty, extend empathy and offer structured options for negotiated due dates as well as additional support to humanize interactions and reduce student feelings of inadequacy

Using Self-Regulation to Reduce Powerlessness

If predictability can be used to reduce anxiety, and vulnerability can be used to reduce shame; then self-regulation can be used to reduce the helplessness felt when overwhelmed with the inadequacy experienced in online learning. Too often adult learners in online environments feel incapable; they feel their options are limited or nonexistent when they need additional support or are confronted by obstacles. Instead of feeling powerless, it is important for students to develop agency with regard to their learning.

In a comprehensive literature review of dozens of studies, self-regulation was repeatedly found to correlate with online students’ persistence and completion with online classes (Khanh and Thanh 2024). Self-agency or self-regulation strategies naturally support students in setting and achieving their own goals, managing their time, and evaluating their own learning. To empower students with agency, consider the following high-impact practices:

Check that Box! – Create clear checklists outlining assignment requirements and pitfalls to improve feeling of control

Optional Opportunities – Build options into assignments to encourage empowerment

Reflective Response Exchange – Add a reflection piece to all assignments to aid in ownership of learning process

Praise Progress – Praise adjustments, revisions, and effort to celebrate student agency

AI with Intentionality – Encourage students to use AI to clarify, explore, and deepen learning while keeping original thinking central to reinforce their sense of capability

Agency and self-regulation work together to counter-balance helplessness. Vulnerability encourages bravery by reducing the shame associated with the risks associated with a return to school and possibilities to fail. Predictability addresses anxiety by stabilizing accessibility and reducing uncertainty. Staying enrolled in school is as much of an emotional decision as it is an academic one, and as instructors, we are positioned to ease the emotional burdens carried by our students through our own high-impact practices and regulations. When students feel confident in navigating learning systems, validated in their personal worth, and empowered instead of powerless, we set them up to not only persist in academics but prevail both academically and emotionally.

Amy Winger, MEd, is an online instructor for the University of Phoenix and American InterContinental University. She holds a BA in English from the University of Iowa and a MEd in English Education from the University of Minnesota. For over 20 years, she has taught English and general education courses and enjoys pioneering the use of tech tools. Prior to that, she taught English at the secondary level. Her academic research primarily focuses on retention strategies, technology tools, and social media implementation in the online classroom. She is also a freelance fiction writer.

References

Dweck, Carol S. 2007. Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. New York: Random House Publishing Group.

Hayat, Ali Asghar, Nahid Barzegar, Hatam Faraji Dehsorkhi, Mehrdad Azimnejadian, Sasan Rostami, Mohammad Hasan Keshavarzi, and Sedigheh Mokhtarpour. 2024. “A Cross-Sectional Study on the Role of Computer Anxiety in Students’ Online Learning.” Journal of Advances in Medical Education & Professionalism 12 (1): 51–56. https://doi.org/10.30476/JAMP.2023.99057

Kaisara, Godwin, Clayton Peel, Cornelius Niemand, and Kelvin Joseph Bwalya. 2024. “Exploring Factors Influencing e-Learning Dropout Rates in the Post-COVID-19 Era.” Information and Communication Technology Education 20 (1): 1-13. https://doi.org/10.4018/IJICTE.348660

Li, Zhiyong, Pengju Guan, Jiaying Li, and Jing Wang. 2024. “Comparing Online and Offline Chinese EFL Learners’ Anxiety and Emotional Engagement.” Acta Psychologica 242 (February): 104114.

title: Why Higher Ed CIOs Must Own Enterprise Data Strategy
summary:
Three departments walk into a meeting with three different enrollment numbers — all of them technically correct.
Most institutions are surrounded by data: reports, dashboards and transactional systems pulling from every corner of campus. And yet, when a leader needs to make a fast, confident decision, the data doesn’t quite deliver. It can be fragmented and inconsistent.
I think about data strategy as everybody’s opportunity and no one area’s problem. Academic affairs, enrollment, student success and finance — each of these teams is using data in smart ways to solve local problems. What a CIO…
full_text:
There’s an opportunity to see how data can inform decisions — not make them — and reduce friction in our processes to improve student outcomes and experiences. It’s becoming easier to talk about these things as we all work together and have the same visibility across the enterprise. They can each positively impact the outcome of higher ed’s mission.

That’s not a technology problem; it’s a visibility problem. And CIOs, by the nature of the role, have visibility across the entire institution in a way almost no one else does.

DISCOVER: Learn about planning, systems and more for a unified data strategy.

Three Things a Unified Data Strategy Unlocks for Higher Education

Throughout universities, there are what I would call “pockets of excellence.” Some people refer to them as silos, but I don’t. I think of them as ways in which people who are incredibly bright and have very specific purposes are doing great things. What CIOs get is a chance to actually incorporate the great ideas in one area that translate well into another area, and the glue behind most of that is data.

Here’s a framing I keep coming back to: Universities are data-rich but information-poor. When I talk with presidents, provosts and boards about why data strategy matters, I come back to three pillars: velocity, cost and resiliency.

Velocity: Unified data helps campus teams move faster

Velocity means being able to move faster with less friction. When data is consistent and accessible, basic questions get answered without weeks of manual reconciliation. Advisers can see which students need support before a situation becomes a crisis. Admissions can respond to shifts in the market in real time. Velocity isn’t about rushing; it’s about removing unnecessary drag.

Cost: Data strategy makes CIOs strategic partners

Cost is about doing more with what you have or doing things differently with what you have. A coherent data strategy surfaces redundant systems, overlapping tools, and inefficient processes quietly consuming budget and staff time. It also helps the CIO shift the conversation from “we’re a cost center” to “we’re a strategic partner in financial sustainability,” which matters when you’re sitting across from a CFO who wants to see ROI.

EXPLORE: Proven change management strategies support successful data governance.

Resiliency: Strong data governance builds institutional resilience

Resiliency is the one that gets underestimated. To me, resiliency means two things: the ability to recover and the ability to pivot. When data is unified and well governed, the institution can change direction quickly — whether that’s due to geopolitical pressure, a financial shock or something nobody saw coming. Fragmented data backs you into a corner. Unified data gives you options.

That gap between data collected and data that actually informs decisions is where the CIO’s biggest opportunity lives right now.

title: Student continuation starts before Welcome Week: rethinking pre-arrival support through an asset-based lens
summary: The post Student continuation starts before Welcome Week: rethinking pre-arrival support through an asset-based lens appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Sarah Yearsley, Senior Lecturer in Education, Childhood and Communities, Liverpool John Moores University shares learning from her research into student continuity.

Supporting student continuation is often associated with what universities do once students have arrived. But what if some of the conditions that enable students to stay are already taking shape before Welcome Week? Drawing together insights from the Advance HE Pre-arrival questionnaire national pilot – Wave One initial results and my doctoral research into student continuation, what we might gain by looking at pre-arrival differently, and by asking not only what challenges students bring with them, but what strengths, relationships and resources they bring too.

When does continuation really begin?

Universities are often prompted to think about continuation when something appears to be going wrong. A student stops attending, misses an assessment, disengages from their learning or starts a conversation about leaving. At this point, institutional processes may trigger interventions designed to re-engage the student and support them to remain.

But are we starting the conversation too late?

Research has shown that continuation is shaped by a complex interaction of academic, social and personal experiences (Tinto, 1993; Thomas, 2012; Kahu and Nelson, 2018). Students also do not arrive at university as blank slates. They bring educational histories, expectations about university life, previous experiences of success and challenge, relationships, responsibilities and existing sources of support.

This is what makes the PAQ particularly interesting. Developed from Michelle Morgan’s work, the PAQ rationale highlights that it is intended to take students on a reflective journey through their previous learning and towards their expectations, concerns and aspirations for higher education. Crucially, it is not simply a data-collection exercise. The information is intended to help institutions listen and respond to incoming students and support their transition into study. Phase one of the national pilot, involving 15 English higher education institutions, has already told us a lot and is providing a much richer picture of the learning histories, expectations, wellbeing concerns and financial pressures students can carry with them into higher education.

For me, this raises a bigger question: what if we started thinking about continuation before there was a continuation problem to solve?

What I learned from students who nearly left

My doctoral research started with a relatively simple question: what might we learn if, instead of asking why students leave university, we ask why they stay?

The students involved in my research had all seriously considered withdrawing from higher education but ultimately continued. What interested me was not only what had brought them to the point of considering withdrawal, but what happened next.

As I brought their experiences together through narrative interviews and Q methodology, it became increasingly clear that there was no single explanation for why a student stayed. Continuation was shaped by combinations of circumstances, relationships, educational experiences, sources of support and students’ own responses to periods of challenge.

This led to me developing my Student Continuity Factors Model.

The model brings together influences identified through the research and positions them along a continuum from lower to greater risk of attrition. These range from academic success, expectations and career aspirations to family and financial circumstances, geographical location, first-generation status, friendship groups, employment, caring responsibilities, health, belonging, course enjoyment and academic and pastoral engagement.

What struck me most when developing the model was that no single factor explained continuation. A challenge in one area could exist alongside something protective elsewhere. A difficult personal circumstance might sit alongside strong motivation. Limited connection to university might coexist with powerful family support. Academic uncertainty could be accompanied by a very clear career goal. It was the wider picture that mattered, and many elements of that picture existed before the student arrived at university.

Looking at pre-arrival differently

This is where there is an interesting conversation to be had between the Student Continuity Factors Model and the PAQ.

The PAQ explores previous learning experiences, motivations, expectations, concerns and attitudes towards study. Many influences represented within my model similarly have roots before university: previous academic experiences, career aspirations, family circumstances, caring responsibilities, geographical location and existing support networks.

Others develop later. Students establish new friendships. They encounter their course and lecturers. They begin to judge whether they belong. Academic and pastoral relationships develop. Course enjoyment changes. The different elements start interacting.

Pre-arrival information can therefore give us something of a starting picture before those new university experiences are added.

The first phase of the national PAQ pilot reinforces why that matters. Findings have identified differences in students’ prior learning and expectations, alongside concerns about finances and wellbeing before arrival. They have also challenged assumptions about areas such as students’ previous academic experience, digital access and literacy, and understanding of virtual learning environments and generative AI.

But there is an important question about what we do with this information.

What if we looked for assets as well as risks?

The Student Continuity Factors Model uses the language of greater and lesser risk of attrition. Understanding risk matters. Universities cannot ignore financial pressures, structural inequalities, caring responsibilities or circumstances that make participation in higher education more difficult.

Since completing the research, I have become increasingly interested in another question: What happens when we look at the same information through an asset-based lens?

The students in my research experienced significant challenges. But their stories were not simply stories about what they lacked. They also spoke about motivation, determination, supportive relationships, previous experiences of overcoming difficulty, connections with peers and staff, and developing a sense of purpose and belonging.

The same principle can be applied to pre-arrival information.

A student with caring responsibilities may face genuine constraints on their time, but those responsibilities might also be connected to a powerful motivation for studying. A commuter student may find participation in campus life more difficult, while retaining strong family, community or employment networks. A student who has struggled in previous education may arrive with concerns about academic study but also considerable persistence and knowledge about how they learn.

So perhaps we need to ask two sets of questions.

Not only, ‘what barriers might this student face?‘, but also: ‘what strengths and resources can they draw upon?‘

Not only, ‘what support will they need?‘, but, ‘what support already exists around them, and where might it need strengthening?‘

This does not mean overlooking disadvantage or expecting students to become more ‘resilient’ in the face of structural barriers. Nor does it transfer responsibility for continuation from universities to individual students.

For me, asset-based awareness is about seeing a more complete picture of the student.

The model helps us think about what might matter. An asset-based approach asks us to think carefully about how we use that knowledge.

Turning information into conversations

Of course, knowing more about incoming students only matters if it changes what we do. This is already central to the rationale for the PAQ. It was designed not simply to gather information, but to allow institutions to respond to students’ expectations and concerns and to enable students themselves to reflect on their forthcoming studies.

At programme level, this might mean using cohort insights to rethink induction, transition activities, how unfamiliar academic expectations are introduced, opportunities for students to establish relationships, or how academic and professional support is communicated.

There may also be opportunities for more individualised support where appropriate and where students have consented to their information being used in this way. The national pilot has deliberately explored how institutions can use PAQ data to support students as well as provide guidance to staff.

Personal tutoring is one possible space for these conversations, but it cannot carry responsibility for continuation alone. Curriculum, teaching, relationships, professional services and institutional structures all contribute to the environment students encounter.

Nor should every PAQ response necessarily trigger an intervention. There is a danger that collecting more information simply creates more sophisticated ways of labelling students as ‘at risk’.

The more interesting possibility is to use pre-arrival information to open rather than close conversations: helping students recognise what they already bring, consider what they might need and identify where new relationships and resources can be developed. The goal is not simply to predict who will stay. It is to create conditions that make continuation more possible.

Continuation starts before Welcome Week

There is one final reason why the PAQ is particularly interesting from a research perspective.

My Student Continuity Factors Model emerged from students studying within a particular period of higher education. I do not think it should be regarded as a finished or fixed account of student continuation. It is in fact designed to allow for such changes and adaptation to occur.

Students change. Higher education changes. The conditions surrounding continuation change.

The emerging PAQ evidence is already challenging assumptions about what incoming students know, expect and worry about. That presents an opportunity for a reciprocal relationship between research and practice. Existing research can help us make sense of what we learn from incoming students, but what those students tell us should also challenge, refine and extend our existing models.

In that sense, implementation itself can become a form of educational scholarship, with practice informing research as well as research informing practice.

Ultimately, the value of pre-arrival information lies not simply in how much universities know about their students, but in what they do differently because they know it. The PAQ gives us an opportunity to listen earlier. The Student Continuity Factors Model provides one way of thinking about why some of what we hear might matter for students’ subsequent journeys. An asset-based approach asks us to listen not only for potential difficulties, but also for the experiences, relationships, motivations and resources upon which students can build.

To conclude, if student continuation begins before students arrive, then the work to support continuation should begin there too.

title: Vibe-coding and co-creation: human-AI collaboration in higher education

full_text:
by Andrew Williams

The debate around artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has largely focused on students. Are they using ChatGPT in assessments? How do we maintain academic integrity? How should teachers and curricula adapt?

Much less attention has been given to academics working with generative AI (GenAI) as a creative collaborator or co-pilot, rather than merely attempting to mitigate its impact. The potential for productive and effective AI collaboration deserves greater consideration because it challenges longstanding assumptions about expertise, creativity and educational design.

Ever since the release of ChatGPT in November 2022, I have been fascinated by how intuitive the interaction with GenAI tools can be and the ease with which ideas can be explored through ordinary conversation. GenAI is a sophisticated technology that allows users to test possibilities, refine outputs, and rapidly turn preliminary concepts into usable material.

My background is in biological sciences, with no grounding or expertise in computer science, software engineering or coding. For me, this technology has helped me overcome technical barriers and allowed me to explore new ways to teach and to develop bespoke educational resources. I envisioned a learning experience for my undergraduate medical science students (studying human genetics and evolution) that moved beyond static textbook diagrams and dry explanations to a more interactive and visually stimulating format. Realising that vision required a simulation that let students tweak parameters, observe real‑time population dynamics, and grasp complex evolutionary ideas.

Traditionally, such a project would rely on grants, external software developers, or months of self‑taught coding. For most of us, the gap between an innovative pedagogical idea and a digital reality was confined by technical expertise. Today, through iterative collaboration with GenAI, natural language can function as a design interface, allowing educators to transform ideas into working educational tools.

I was also intrigued by the ever improving, and often publicised, capabilities of GenAI tools as coding agents. With no coding experience myself, I decided to try my hand at ‘vibe-coding’.

Natural language as a design interface

‘Vibe-coding’ is an emerging term within technology communities that describes a process where functional intent is communicated via natural language prompts, allowing AI to generate and refine code. This allows the user to focus on what the tool should do rather than how it must be coded. Essentially, ‘vibe-coding’ involves directing the AI to write and co-develop code aligned with your vision and pedagogical objectives. In other words – no code, no problem!

My recent research describes an iterative prompting strategy and the outcomes of a human-AI collaboration to create an interactive simulation that models certain aspects of evolution (Williams, 2026a). Instead of learning JavaScript or working with software developers, I co-created an application with ChatGPT using only natural language prompting. The result was a browser-based simulation capable of supporting inquiry-based learning and formative assessment in undergraduate education.

Rather than blindly generating content based on loosely defined instructions, the human-AI collaboration involved a structured iterative prompting strategy, careful testing of AI-generated output and re-prompting until the desired aims of the project were met. This enabled the creation of an interactive simulation in which students could investigate biological systems, manipulate variables, export datasets and construct evidence-based explanations (figure 1). This allowed students to move beyond consuming information, to generating and interpreting data themselves in real-time.

Figure 1. Snapshot of ‘Survival Island’ – an interactive simulation.

The Illusion of automated expertise

There is a prevailing narrative that AI democratises expertise, in that it allows anyone to do anything more quickly and with less effort. My experience of ‘vibe-coding’ suggested something different. The credibility of the final simulation depended on actively embedding disciplinary expertise directly into the co-design process.

While the AI had removed the technical barrier (the coding), it had increased the importance of my academic expertise and oversight. The AI could generate a thousand lines of code in seconds, but it couldn’t tell me if the code represented a plausible scientific simulation. My epistemic judgement was required to verify the AI-generated output. The final student-ready simulation required multiple rounds of iteration, testing and re-prompting, until the collaboration achieved a credible and biologically grounded application suitable for teaching.

Rather than replacing my expertise, ChatGPT provided capabilities I do not possess: writing HTML; JavaScript; debugging code. I contributed disciplinary knowledge, pedagogical intent and continuous evaluation. Every feature reflected educational decisions rather than technical ones. The simulation succeeded because the educational need was clearly defined before AI generated the code.

Higher education has often treated GenAI as an automated assistant or as a problem to be mitigated. Increasingly, it may be more productive to think of AI as a collaborator whose contributions depend upon human judgement. Expertise remains indispensable, as humans ultimately remain responsible for judging whether outputs are educationally, scientifically and ethically sound.

Beyond the prompt: the AI literacy gap

Universities have understandably invested considerable effort in developing student AI literacy. This project led me to a broader appreciation of the need to promote teacher AI literacy across higher education, a critical area often overlooked.

AI literacy for teachers is not just about knowing how to write a good prompt or choosing the best online GenAI tool. Rather, it is a multi-dimensional competency that considers foundational knowledge (prompting, tool use), ethical, emotional and technical proficiencies. For educators to co-create teaching resources in collaboration with AI, for example through vibe-coding, more than technical curiosity is required.

The iterative ‘vibe-coding’ process I followed mirrors the ‘critical evaluation’, ‘epistemic’ and ‘innovation’ dimensions of an integrated AI literacy framework for higher education teachers (Williams, 2026b). This recently published conceptual framework comprises eight core AI literacy dimensions, which you can access in full using the link.

In the current context, the important AI literacy dimensions include:

Critical evaluation: the ability to treat the AI model as a “black box” and rigorously verify outputs against authoritative sources.

Epistemic authority: a clear understanding of the probabilistic nature of GenAI and the domain-specific expertise to judge AI output, thereby retaining human agency during interactions with AI.

Innovation mindset: the willingness to move from being a consumer of tools to a co-creator of bespoke learning environments, including an understanding of how to collaborate effectively with GenAI.

These are becoming essential academic capabilities rather than optional technical skills. This transition presents considerable challenges, as academic practice has historically been predicated on either individual resource creation or the outsourcing of technical development to third parties. GenAI now enables academics to become directors of increasingly sophisticated creative processes. They define the educational challenge, AI performs the technical implementation, and academics evaluate and verify the final outcome.

As technical production becomes easier with GenAI, educational judgement becomes increasingly important. Our value is no longer found in the technical labour of production, but in our ability to define the educational challenge, critique the iterations, and curate the final outcome. The “vibe” we are coding is our pedagogical intent.

Key takeaways

AI is a tool, not a replacement.

Human-AI collaboration enables pedagogical creativity.

‘Vibe-coding’ uses AI’s coding capabilities but demands epistemic oversight.

Teacher AI literacy is multi‑dimensional.

Institutional support is required to build that AI literacy.

GenAI is redefining the landscape of higher education, not through incremental improvements to traditional teaching materials, but by enabling entirely new educational content to be created. However, despite the promises of this new technological revolution, we still need robust evidence about student learning gains, engagement, accessibility and the sustainability of AI-generated educational resources.

It is easy to provide AI tools for HE educators to use. The challenge is to give educators the technical, critical and ethical literacy required to use them effectively.

Andrew Williams is a Professor (Teaching) in the Faculty of Medical Sciences at UCL. He teaches immunology and cell and molecular biology to undergraduate and postgraduate students. His research aims to explore the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on assessment and learning in higher education and the ways in which we can promote student and staff AI literacy.

title: El voto latinoamericano, ¿ideológico o pragmático?
summary:
Pablo Vommaro y otros analizan la actualidad regional en DW

La entrada El voto latinoamericano, ¿ideológico o pragmático? se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
Los últimos comicios en América Latina confirman una creciente ola derechista. ¿Es parte del movimiento pendular, que vemos entre los extremos políticos, o nuevas motivaciones guían a los electores?

De derecha a izquierda, y viceversa, el péndulo se inclina en las elecciones en América Latina y esta vez de forma marcada. En contraste con la pasada marea rosa de gobiernos progresistas de izquierda, ahora es el turno de la ola conservadora de derecha, que se está consolidando gracias a los últimos triunfos en Ecuador, Chile, Bolivia, Perú y Colombia.

«Es un péndulo, pero es además un péndulo anti establishment, porque las recetas antiguas que se habían dado ya no les sirven a los electorados y buscan nuevas alternativas fuera de lo establecido», dice a DW Javiera Arce, investigadora del Centro de Estudios para la Gestión Pública de la Universidad de Valparaíso, Chile.

«Algunos análisis muestran que el cambio es lo que ha determinado el voto en muchas de las elecciones de los últimos años en América Latina. A veces, cuando aparecen opciones autoritarias o reaccionarias, tiene que ver más con la búsqueda de un cambio respecto a lo que había, que con una adhesión programática a la ultraderecha», señala a DW Pablo Vommaro, director ejecutivo del Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales (CLACSO).

En opinión de Arce, los partidos políticos se han vuelto «menos ideologizados y más bien pragmáticos, basados en un consenso centrista». Con ello, ha bajado la disputa ideológica y se han concentrado en nuevas causas. «Se enfrentan por temas más accesorios y demandas más inmediatas, pequeñas y de nicho», añade la doctora en Ciencia Política, quien estima que las conexiones de la población con los partidos se han debilitado: «Parece ser que no canalizan precisamente los afectos de la ciudadanía. Por lo tanto, hemos tenido un revival de las antiguas demandas materiales, como tener seguridad ciudadana y seguridad económica».

En opinión de Hans-Jürgen Burchardt, la duración de los ciclos del péndulo es variable y no sabemos cuánto pueda extenderse a mediano y largo plazo. «Hay que reconocer, por un lado, que el centro progresista no logró cumplir con su promesa más importante, que ha sido la redistribución, pero no solamente por cuestiones de justicia social, sino por hacer más productivos a los países y, a través de eso, mejorar las condiciones de vida y de trabajo. Esa ha sido una gran desilusión de estos gobiernos, y de eso se ha aprovechado la derecha en algunos momentos», observa el catedrático de Relaciones Internacionales de la Universidad de Kassel, en diálogo con DW.

Por otra parte, pone el ejemplo de la última elección en Chile. El debate se centró en la seguridad, un tema muy presente en los medios, a pesar de que el nivel de alarma no se condice con las cifras. Como la migración, la inseguridad es un tópico que prioriza la derecha, por sobre preocupaciones como salud, educación o pensiones.

Lucha por capturar las subjetividades

Si bien persisten disputas por agendas materiales en algunos países, como el trabajo, la vivienda o la salud -en la elección de Milei en Argentina, por ejemplo, fue la inflación o el valor del dólar-, «la disputa situada en el terreno de las subjetividades, de lo afectivo, lo emocional y los gustos ha cobrado mayor importancia y mayor espacio en la definición de las contiendas electorales en los últimos años», explica Vommaro.

«Hay una disputa de sentido, que inclusive en algunas fuerzas de ultraderecha se enuncia como batalla cultural», evalúa el profesor e investigador de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA). Esto incide en la configuración de las subjetividades de las y los votantes, y se articula con la sensación de descontento que prima en estos escenarios. En la disputa por influenciar las percepciones, el mundo digital y las redes sociales tienen un rol importante, así como la estrategia de las desinformaciones, las noticias falsas o creadas con IA a partir de datos no verídicos.

A esta situación contribuye «la creciente incertidumbre en la que vivimos, un mundo donde parece que nada es seguro, que todo se puede conmover, desde la tierra que tiembla hasta la pandemia y las guerras. La incertidumbre respecto al futuro es muy fuerte en las nuevas generaciones. También contribuye a que la dimensión afectiva cobre mayor valor que en décadas anteriores», expone el director ejecutivo de CLACSO.

El presidente de Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, ante un micrófono, con la banda presidencial, durante el 88.º aniversario de la Policía Nacional ecuatoriana.

Por su parte, Burchardt apunta a que «ningún político tiene respuestas, y la derecha no las tiene, pero logra capitalizar el miedo, aunque no se puede resolver la cuestión de la seguridad a través de un aumento de represión policial o militar. Se necesitan otras respuestas».

Al respecto, el director del Centro de investigación Käte Hamburger Kolleg, de la Universidad de Kassel, distingue diferencias entre los países: Argentina depende mucho del FMI y de los créditos, y ante la amenaza de falta de apoyo de Trump, parte de la población decidió votar por Milei. Pero en Brasil, en tanto, Lula tuvo una postura clara de defender su autonomía, y ganó popularidad.

Votantes menos fieles y más pragmáticos

Al observar los vaivenes de las elecciones latinoamericanas del último tiempo, pareciera que los electores ya no son fieles a una tendencia política, sino que se mueven por otros intereses. «Sienten que tampoco la política ha sido fiel con ellos y con sus demandas, por lo que acomodan sus preferencias, maximizando sus opciones», indica Arce.

Para Vommaro, «hoy en día el voto se define menos por ideología, adhesión a un programa o fidelidad partidaria, y se decide más por condiciones materiales y subjetivas más inmediatas. El voto es más pragmático en el sentido de más contingente, menos fidelizado a algunas opciones. Existen también votos fidelizados, por supuesto, pero se van diluyendo cada vez más».

Al mismo tiempo, «es más emocional, afectivo y vinculado con otras afinidades que no tienen que ver directamente con una adhesión programática o ideológica, sino con sensaciones y percepciones, que muchas veces son más bien negativas, es decir, de malestar, de desilusión y desencanto. Y entonces aparece una búsqueda de cambio», plantea el académico de la UBA.

«Se podría decir que votan en contra de algo: por ejemplo, en Chile, en contra del fascismo de Kast en 2021, o en contra del comunismo de Jeannette Jara en 2025, o en Colombia recién, o el voto antiperonista con Milei en 2023».

En ese sentido, Burchardt ve que en Argentina «el último gobierno de Alberto Fernández fue una desilusión para gran parte de las personas. No solo creó una alta inflación, sino también aumentó el desempleo entre los jóvenes, y ellos se sintieron más desilusionados del gobierno progresista que de las propias ideas y objetivos de la derecha».

¿Estamos en una era posideológica?

En medio de este panorama, la pregunta es si pasó el tiempo de las ideologías. Arce precisa: «No hablaría de posideología. Estas derechas que tenemos son extremadamente ideológicas. Estamos viviendo una lucha descarnada por la ideología y es una ideología completamente distinta».

Por su parte, Burchardt considera que pasó «hasta cierto punto». «Si hablamos de la izquierda o de los partidos progresistas, les falta una narrativa de una promesa de futuro, y si los políticos no pueden ofrecer nada, significa que tenemos una desideologización, pero no como un proceso de nueva política, sino de incompetencia de accionar una narrativa». Asimismo, estima que la derecha tiene la capacidad de «canalizar, capitalizar el miedo (de la ciudadanía) y eso es lo que está haciendo al ganar elecciones, aunque no tiene respuesta para nada. Y eso no es una ideologización».

«No sé si la ideología quedó atrás, porque inclusive desde los discursos dominantes se agita ideología, cuando se tilda de ‘comunista’ o ‘socialista’, o hace unos años, de ‘castrista’ o ‘chavista’, o cuando se ponen algunos países, como Cuba o Venezuela, como los ejemplos negativos, los ‘cucos’ y las causas de todos los males. Esos discursos son fuertemente ideológicos», advierte Vommaro. No obstante, reitera que las ideologías y las adhesiones programáticas han perdido peso específico en la contienda política, al tiempo que crecen las adhesiones afectivas, emocionales y más subjetivas.

Victoria Dannemann

Los últimos comicios en América Latina confirman una creciente ola derechista. ¿Es parte del movimiento pendular, que vemos entre los extremos políticos, o nuevas motivaciones guían a los electores?

De derecha a izquierda, y viceversa, el péndulo se inclina en las elecciones en América Latina y esta vez de forma marcada. En contraste con la pasada marea rosa de gobiernos progresistas de izquierda, ahora es el turno de la ola conservadora de derecha, que se está consolidando gracias a los últimos triunfos en Ecuador, Chile, Bolivia, Perú y Colombia.

«Es un péndulo, pero es además un péndulo anti establishment, porque las recetas antiguas que se habían dado ya no les sirven a los electorados y buscan nuevas alternativas fuera de lo establecido», dice a DW Javiera Arce, investigadora del Centro de Estudios para la Gestión Pública de la Universidad de Valparaíso, Chile.

«Algunos análisis muestran que el cambio es lo que ha determinado el voto en muchas de las elecciones de los últimos años en América Latina. A veces, cuando aparecen opciones autoritarias o reaccionarias, tiene que ver más con la búsqueda de un cambio respecto a lo que había, que con una adhesión programática a la ultraderecha», señala a DW Pablo Vommaro, director ejecutivo del Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales (CLACSO).

En opinión de Arce, los partidos políticos se han vuelto «menos ideologizados y más bien pragmáticos, basados en un consenso centrista». Con ello, ha bajado la disputa ideológica y se han concentrado en nuevas causas. «Se enfrentan por temas más accesorios y demandas más inmediatas, pequeñas y de nicho», añade la doctora en Ciencia Política, quien estima que las conexiones de la población con los partidos se han debilitado: «Parece ser que no canalizan precisamente los afectos de la ciudadanía. Por lo tanto, hemos tenido un revival de las antiguas demandas materiales, como tener seguridad ciudadana y seguridad económica».

En opinión de Hans-Jürgen Burchardt, la duración de los ciclos del péndulo es variable y no sabemos cuánto pueda extenderse a mediano y largo plazo. «Hay que reconocer, por un lado, que el centro progresista no logró cumplir con su promesa más importante, que ha sido la redistribución, pero no solamente por cuestiones de justicia social, sino por hacer más productivos a los países y, a través de eso, mejorar las condiciones de vida y de trabajo. Esa ha sido una gran desilusión de estos gobiernos, y de eso se ha aprovechado la derecha en algunos momentos», observa el catedrático de Relaciones Internacionales de la Universidad de Kassel, en diálogo con DW.

Por otra parte, pone el ejemplo de la última elección en Chile. El debate se centró en la seguridad, un tema muy presente en los medios, a pesar de que el nivel de alarma no se condice con las cifras. Como la migración, la inseguridad es un tópico que prioriza la derecha, por sobre preocupaciones como salud, educación o pensiones.

Lucha por capturar las subjetividades

Si bien persisten disputas por agendas materiales en algunos países, como el trabajo, la vivienda o la salud -en la elección de Milei en Argentina, por ejemplo, fue la inflación o el valor del dólar-, «la disputa situada en el terreno de las subjetividades, de lo afectivo, lo emocional y los gustos ha cobrado mayor importancia y mayor espacio en la definición de las contiendas electorales en los últimos años», explica Vommaro.

«Hay una disputa de sentido, que inclusive en algunas fuerzas de ultraderecha se enuncia como batalla cultural», evalúa el profesor e investigador de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA). Esto incide en la configuración de las subjetividades de las y los votantes, y se articula con la sensación de descontento que prima en estos escenarios. En la disputa por influenciar las percepciones, el mundo digital y las redes sociales tienen un rol importante, así como la estrategia de las desinformaciones, las noticias falsas o creadas con IA a partir de datos no verídicos.

A esta situación contribuye «la creciente incertidumbre en la que vivimos, un mundo donde parece que nada es seguro, que todo se puede conmover, desde la tierra que tiembla hasta la pandemia y las guerras. La incertidumbre respecto al futuro es muy fuerte en las nuevas generaciones. También contribuye a que la dimensión afectiva cobre mayor valor que en décadas anteriores», expone el director ejecutivo de CLACSO.

El presidente de Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, ante un micrófono, con la banda presidencial, durante el 88.º aniversario de la Policía Nacional ecuatoriana.

Por su parte, Burchardt apunta a que «ningún político tiene respuestas, y la derecha no las tiene, pero logra capitalizar el miedo, aunque no se puede resolver la cuestión de la seguridad a través de un aumento de represión policial o militar. Se necesitan otras respuestas».

Al respecto, el director del Centro de investigación Käte Hamburger Kolleg, de la Universidad de Kassel, distingue diferencias entre los países: Argentina depende mucho del FMI y de los créditos, y ante la amenaza de falta de apoyo de Trump, parte de la población decidió votar por Milei. Pero en Brasil, en tanto, Lula tuvo una postura clara de defender su autonomía, y ganó popularidad.

Votantes menos fieles y más pragmáticos

Al observar los vaivenes de las elecciones latinoamericanas del último tiempo, pareciera que los electores ya no son fieles a una tendencia política, sino que se mueven por otros intereses. «Sienten que tampoco la política ha sido fiel con ellos y con sus demandas, por lo que acomodan sus preferencias, maximizando sus opciones», indica Arce.

Para Vommaro, «hoy en día el voto se define menos por ideología, adhesión a un programa o fidelidad partidaria, y se decide más por condiciones materiales y subjetivas más inmediatas. El voto es más pragmático en el sentido de más contingente, menos fidelizado a algunas opciones. Existen también votos fidelizados, por supuesto, pero se van diluyendo cada vez más».

Al mismo tiempo, «es más emocional, afectivo y vinculado con otras afinidades que no tienen que ver directamente con una adhesión programática o ideológica, sino con sensaciones y percepciones, que muchas veces son más bien negativas, es decir, de malestar, de desilusión y desencanto. Y entonces aparece una búsqueda de cambio», plantea el académico de la UBA.

«Se podría decir que votan en contra de algo: por ejemplo, en Chile, en contra del fascismo de Kast en 2021, o en contra del comunismo de Jeannette Jara en 2025, o en Colombia recién, o el voto antiperonista con Milei en 2023».

En ese sentido, Burchardt ve que en Argentina «el último gobierno de Alberto Fernández fue una desilusión para gran parte de las personas. No solo creó una alta inflación, sino también aumentó el desempleo entre los jóvenes, y ellos se sintieron más desilusionados del gobierno progresista que de las propias ideas y objetivos de la derecha».

¿Estamos en una era posideológica?

En medio de este panorama, la pregunta es si pasó el tiempo de las ideologías. Arce precisa: «No hablaría de posideología. Estas derechas que tenemos son extremadamente ideológicas. Estamos viviendo una lucha descarnada por la ideología y es una ideología completamente distinta».

Por su parte, Burchardt considera que pasó «hasta cierto punto». «Si hablamos de la izquierda o de los partidos progresistas, les falta una narrativa de una promesa de futuro, y si los políticos no pueden ofrecer nada, significa que tenemos una desideologización, pero no como un proceso de nueva política, sino de incompetencia de accionar una narrativa». Asimismo, estima que la derecha tiene la capacidad de «canalizar, capitalizar el miedo (de la ciudadanía) y eso es lo que está haciendo al ganar elecciones, aunque no tiene respuesta para nada. Y eso no es una ideologización».

«No sé si la ideología quedó atrás, porque inclusive desde los discursos dominantes se agita ideología, cuando se tilda de ‘comunista’ o ‘socialista’, o hace unos años, de ‘castrista’ o ‘chavista’, o cuando se ponen algunos países, como Cuba o Venezuela, como los ejemplos negativos, los ‘cucos’ y las causas de todos los males. Esos discursos son fuertemente ideológicos», advierte Vommaro. No obstante, reitera que las ideologías y las adhesiones programáticas han perdido peso específico en la contienda política, al tiempo que crecen las adhesiones afectivas, emocionales y más subjetivas.

Victoria Dannemann

L’esponente dell’esecutivo traccia il percorso e anche il punto su questa prima parte del programma che ha visto diverse imprese impegnate in settori differenti affrontare la sfida delle fiere e degli scenari extraisolani. «Sicuramente il primo bilancio sui progetti è positivo -dice -. Abbiamo organizzato il sistema delle nostre imprese in attività di presenza nell’ambito di fiere nazionali e internazionali importanti, di grande rilevanza». Non solo, per l’esponente dell’esecutivo «il ritorno è sicuramente positivo». « È positivo per il fatto che mettere a disposizione platee così rilevanti dal punto di vista delle relazioni può costituire per il nostro sistema produttivo un volano di sviluppo e di crescita molto importante».

A giocare la carta dello sviluppo e crescita guardando ai mercati nazionali e internazionali ci sono settori come il marmo e quello dei lapidei, ambito che in Sardegna è rappresentato da una settantina di imprese. Ci sono poi le startup e le altre aziende impegnate nel settore dell’innovazione. Non meno importanti poi le aziende che operano nel settore dell’enogastronomia e che giocano la carta delle esportazioni internazionali con un’attenzione particolare ai mercati orientali e a quelli statunitensi. «A oggi siamo sicuramente molto soddisfatti, ovviamente ci sono molti margini di crescita». Quanto al futuro, l’assessore aggiunge: «Sicuramente per il futuro dobbiamo, così come stiamo facendo, calibrare le nostre attività di promozione delle nostre imprese nell’ambito nazionale internazionale, andando a vedere quello che saranno i programmi di sviluppo industriale della nostra regione».

C’è poi un intero settore su cui la Regione e l’assessorato intendono puntare. «Cito un esempio importante su cui stiamo lavorando - prosegue - si tratta della valorizzazione di tutto il settore delle materie prime critiche, delle terre rare, su cui sarà assolutamente importante avere a disposizione delle platee a livello internazionale importanti, dove poterci misurare rispetto a quello che la Sardegna e le proprie prese possono dare su un settore così importante per lo sviluppo regionale, nazionale, ma così strategiche a livello internazionale».
